Cabernet Sauvignon

**Color:** red · **Body:** full · **Tannin:** high · **Acidity:** medium-high
**Signature flavors:** blackcurrant (cassis), cedar, graphite, tobacco, mint or bell pepper in cooler sites
**Home base:** Bordeaux Left Bank (Médoc, Pessac-Léognan), where it is usually blended with Merlot and Cabernet Franc.
**Also thrives in:** Napa Valley, Chile (Maipo, Colchagua), Australia (Coonawarra, Margaret River), Washington State, Tuscany (in "Super Tuscan" blends).
**Character:** The world's most planted quality red grape. Small, thick-skinned berries give deep color, firm tannin, and serious ageing capacity. A late ripener — it needs warmth, which is why it struggles in marginal climates and why cool-vintage examples can taste green.
**Ageing potential:** Excellent; top examples improve for 10–30+ years. Entry-level bottles are best within 5.
**Serve at:** 16–18°C. Young, tannic examples benefit from decanting.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a structured, classic red for steak, lamb, or hard cheeses; wants a wine to cellar; or asks for "a serious red."

Merlot

**Color:** red · **Body:** medium-full · **Tannin:** medium · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** plum, black cherry, chocolate, bay leaf; fleshy and soft in texture
**Home base:** Bordeaux Right Bank (Pomerol, Saint-Émilion), where it is the most planted grape.
**Also thrives in:** northeast Italy, Chile, California, Washington State.
**Character:** Cabernet Sauvignon's traditional blending partner — earlier ripening, plumper, lower in tannin, and approachable younger. On clay-rich Right Bank soils it reaches its most opulent, velvety expression. Underripe Merlot turns green and weedy, which fed its unfair reputation as a lesser grape.
**Ageing potential:** Top Pomerol/Saint-Émilion 10–25 years; most varietal Merlot 3–8 years.
**Serve at:** 15–17°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a smooth, generous red without aggressive tannin; a crowd-pleasing red for roast chicken, pork, or mushroom dishes; or a gentler entry into Bordeaux.

Pinot Noir

**Color:** red · **Body:** light-medium · **Tannin:** low-medium · **Acidity:** high
**Signature flavors:** red cherry, raspberry, violet, forest floor and game with age; pale to mid-ruby color
**Home base:** Burgundy's Côte d'Or — the benchmark every other region chases.
**Also thrives in:** Oregon (Willamette Valley), New Zealand (Central Otago, Martinborough), Germany (as Spätburgunder), coastal California (Sonoma Coast, Sta. Rita Hills), Ontario's Niagara Peninsula and Prince Edward County.
**Character:** Thin-skinned, early ripening, and famously fussy — too much heat and it ripens fast without developing its haunting aromatics. The most transparent major grape: it broadcasts site differences, which is exactly why Burgundy's vineyard hierarchy exists. Rarely blended in still wine; with Chardonnay and Pinot Meunier it is the backbone of champagne.
**Ageing potential:** Village-level 3–8 years; premier/grand cru Burgundy 10–25 years.
**Serve at:** 14–16°C — cooler than most reds; the Burgundian tradition is nearly cellar temperature.
**Recommend when:** the user wants an elegant, aromatic red; a red for salmon, duck, or mushroom dishes; a red for someone who "doesn't like heavy reds"; or a food-versatile bottle for a mixed table.

Syrah / Shiraz

**Color:** red · **Body:** full · **Tannin:** medium-high · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** black pepper, dark fruit, dark chocolate, olive, smoked meat; dense and savory in the Rhône, richer and sweeter-fruited as Shiraz in Australia
**Home base:** Northern Rhône (Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie, Cornas, Saint-Joseph).
**Also thrives in:** Australia (Barossa, McLaren Vale, cooler Victoria), Chile, South Africa, Washington State, and throughout southern France in blends.
**Character:** One grape, two identities. In its northern Rhône home it makes dark, long-lived, savory wines — Côte-Rôtie traditionally co-fermented with a splash of white Viognier for perfume. In warm Australia, as Shiraz, it becomes dense, rich, and potent, though cooler regions preserve the telltale pepper note. Ripe examples always finish with a savory kick.
**Ageing potential:** Top northern Rhône and Barossa 10–30 years; everyday bottles 3–7 years.
**Serve at:** 16–18°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a bold, savory red; something for barbecue, grilled meats, or peppery dishes; or an alternative to Cabernet with more spice and less austerity.

Grenache / Garnacha

**Color:** red · **Body:** medium-full · **Tannin:** low-medium · **Acidity:** low-medium
**Signature flavors:** strawberry, raspberry, white pepper, dried herbs (garrigue); pale color, generous alcohol
**Home base:** Southern Rhône — the lead grape of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, usually blended with Syrah and Mourvèdre (the "GSM" trio).
**Also thrives in:** Spain (Campo de Borja, Gredos, Priorat), Roussillon, Sardinia (as Cannonau), Australia and California, where old bushvines are increasingly prized.
**Character:** Heat-loving and drought-tolerant, Grenache needs full ripeness to express itself, which pushes alcohol high. Pale in color but rich in fruit, it is also the base of excellent rosé (Provence, Navarra) and the fortified sweet wines of Roussillon. Old-vine Grenache from Spain is one of wine's great value plays.
**Ageing potential:** Most 3–8 years; top Châteauneuf and Priorat 10–20.
**Serve at:** 15–17°C; rosé versions well chilled at 8–10°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a warm, fruit-forward red without heavy tannin; a match for Mediterranean food, lamb, or spiced dishes; or a serious rosé.

Tempranillo

**Color:** red · **Body:** medium-full · **Tannin:** medium · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** red and black fruit, tobacco leaf, leather, dill and coconut when aged in American oak
**Home base:** Spain — the backbone of Rioja and Ribera del Duero.
**Also thrives in:** Portugal (as Tinta Roriz in port and Douro table wines, Aragonês in Alentejo), with scattered plantings worldwide.
**Character:** Spain's flagship grape travels under many aliases: Tinto Fino, Cencibel, Ull de Llebre. Early budding makes it frost-prone and its thin skins are rot-sensitive, but in the right sites it delivers ageworthy, distinctive reds. Traditional Rioja is defined by long oak ageing — the Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva ladder — while Ribera del Duero leans darker and more powerful.
**Ageing potential:** Gran Reserva Rioja can go 15–30 years; most bottles 4–10.
**Serve at:** 15–17°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a savory, oak-kissed red; a match for roast lamb, jamón, or grilled vegetables; or an ageworthy red that's often better value than Bordeaux or Burgundy.

Sangiovese

**Color:** red · **Body:** medium · **Tannin:** medium-high · **Acidity:** high
**Signature flavors:** sour cherry, tomato leaf, dried herbs, balsamic; fairly pale, tangy, lively
**Home base:** Central Italy — Chianti Classico, Montalcino (as Brunello), Montepulciano (as Prugnolo Gentile), Maremma (as Morellino).
**Character:** Italy's most planted grape and both its workhorse and its potential hero. Overcropped clones make light, tart wine; great sites and serious farming make wines of real depth and longevity. Once diluted with white grapes under old Chianti rules and once scorned in favor of Cabernet and Merlot, 100% Sangiovese is now both officially sanctioned and widely admired. Its high acidity makes it one of the great food wines.
**Ageing potential:** Brunello and top Chianti Classico Riserva 10–25 years; everyday Chianti 2–6.
**Serve at:** 15–17°C.
**Recommend when:** the user is eating anything with tomato, pasta, pizza, or salumi; wants a high-acid red for food; or asks for Italian classics.

Nebbiolo

**Color:** red · **Body:** full (in structure, not color) · **Tannin:** very high · **Acidity:** high
**Signature flavors:** tar and roses, dried cherry, licorice, truffle; deceptively pale garnet color
**Home base:** Piedmont, northwest Italy — Barolo and Barbaresco.
**Character:** A paradox: pale as Pinot Noir, tannic as anything on earth. Named for the fog (nebbia) that blankets Piedmont in late autumn, it is one of the latest-ripening major grapes and intensely site-sensitive. Young Barolo can be austere and unyielding; with age it unfolds into one of wine's most haunting bouquets. Alto Piemonte and Valtellina offer lighter, earlier-drinking expressions.
**Ageing potential:** Barolo/Barbaresco genuinely need 8–10 years and can run 20–40.
**Serve at:** 16–18°C, decanted when young.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a profound, cellar-worthy red; a match for truffle, braised beef, or rich risotto; or is a Burgundy lover ready for Piedmont.

Malbec

**Color:** red · **Body:** full · **Tannin:** medium · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** blackberry, violet, cocoa, sweet spice; velvety and concentrated in Argentina, more rustic and gamey in Cahors
**Home base (adopted):** Mendoza, Argentina — where it became the national grape.
**Home base (original):** Southwest France; the dominant grape of Cahors, where it's known as Côt or Auxerrois.
**Character:** A conundrum grape: long a minor blender across Southwest France (including Bordeaux), it found its true home in Mendoza's high-altitude desert, where intense sunlight and cool nights yield gloriously velvety, lively, high-extract wines. Ambitious Cahors producers now take Mendoza's best as their model rather than the other way around.
**Ageing potential:** Top single-vineyard Mendoza 8–15 years; most 3–7.
**Serve at:** 16–18°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a plush, dark, crowd-pleasing red; anything involving grilled or roasted beef; or a value alternative to Napa Cabernet.

Cabernet Franc

**Color:** red · **Body:** medium · **Tannin:** medium · **Acidity:** medium-high
**Signature flavors:** raspberry, red currant, pencil shavings, leafy/herbal lift; aromatic, refreshing, rarely heavy
**Home base:** Loire Valley (Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur-Champigny) and Bordeaux's Right Bank, where it blends with Merlot in Saint-Émilion.
**Also thrives in:** Ontario's Niagara Peninsula (a signature red for Canadian icewine and table wine), New Zealand, Long Island, Washington State, northeast Italy.
**Character:** A genetic parent of Cabernet Sauvignon — softer, earlier ripening, and far more cold-hardy, which is why it's planted as insurance in the Médoc and why it excels in cool climates like the Loire and Ontario. At its silky Chinon apogee it is one of the most refreshing serious reds in the world.
**Ageing potential:** Most 3–8 years; top Loire and Saint-Émilion 10–20.
**Serve at:** 14–16°C, lightly chilled in summer.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a lighter, aromatic, food-friendly red; something for charcuterie, roast poultry, or goat cheese; or a Canadian-grown red with pedigree.

Mourvèdre / Monastrell / Mataro

**Color:** red · **Body:** full · **Tannin:** high · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** blackberry, meat, leather, wild herbs; animal, alcoholic, tannic
**Home base:** Bandol in Provence — its most noble expression — and east-central Spain as Monastrell.
**Character:** Not famous, but vital: throughout southern France and South Australia it adds flesh and structure to Grenache-Syrah blends. It needs serious heat to ripen and careful winemaking, as it's prone to reductive (sulfurous) notes. In California and Australia it was long overlooked under the name Mataro before a renaissance restored its French name and reputation.
**Ageing potential:** Bandol 10–20 years; most blends 5–10.
**Serve at:** 16–18°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a wild, savory, structured red; a match for game, lamb stew, or aged cheeses; or already loves GSM blends.

Zinfandel / Primitivo

**Color:** red · **Body:** full · **Tannin:** medium · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** warm bramble berries, dried fig, sweet spice; high alcohol, often a touch of sweetness
**Home base:** California, especially old vines in Sonoma; genetically identical to Puglia's Primitivo, and originally from Croatia.
**Character:** Regarded as California's own grape for a century until DNA analysis traced it across the Adriatic. The vine ripens unevenly — some berries reach jammy super-ripeness while others lag — so Zin can hit 16–17% alcohol. Old-vine bottlings can be genuinely great; much of the crop historically went into the off-dry pink "White Zinfandel."
**Ageing potential:** Best old-vine examples 8–15 years; most 3–6.
**Serve at:** 16–17°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a rich, ripe, spicy red; barbecue, ribs, or burgers are on the menu; or they like bold fruit over savory austerity.

Gamay

**Color:** red · **Body:** light · **Tannin:** low · **Acidity:** high
**Signature flavors:** fresh red berries, banana and bubblegum in carbonic styles, peony, crushed stone in cru Beaujolais
**Home base:** Beaujolais, on granite hills south of Burgundy.
**Character:** The grape of joy. Basic Beaujolais and Nouveau are light, gulpable, and best young; the ten crus (Morgon, Fleurie, Moulin-à-Vent, and others) make structured, terroir-driven wines that can rival village Burgundy at a fraction of the price. A darling of the natural wine movement and increasingly planted in Ontario and Niagara, where the climate suits it.
**Ageing potential:** Nouveau: months. Crus: 3–10 years.
**Serve at:** 12–14°C — genuinely chillable.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a chillable, low-tannin red; a picnic or apéro wine; a red for charcuterie or roast chicken; or a natural-wine-adjacent pick.

Chardonnay

**Color:** white · **Body:** medium-full · **Acidity:** medium-high · **Oak affinity:** very high
**Signature flavors:** apple and citrus (cool climates) through peach and melon (warm); butter, hazelnut, and brioche from oak and lees work
**Home base:** Burgundy — from steely Chablis to opulent Meursault and Montrachet.
**Also thrives in:** Champagne (as the sole grape of Blanc de Blancs), California, Australia, Oregon, New Zealand, Ontario — it grows nearly everywhere.
**Character:** The world's most famous white grape precisely because it has no loud flavor of its own: it is a canvas for place and winemaking. It can be lean and mineral, rich and buttery, sparkling, or sweet. Its early budding risks spring frost (Chablis famously fights this with water-spray ice protection). Malolactic conversion and barrel fermentation are the levers behind its creamy styles.
**Ageing potential:** Grand cru white Burgundy 10–20 years; Chablis ages on acidity; most commercial Chardonnay is best within 3–5.
**Serve at:** 10–13°C — richer styles at the warmer end.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a versatile white for roast chicken, lobster, or creamy dishes; asks for "a buttery white" (oaked) or "a crisp but not tart white" (unoaked Chablis-style).

Sauvignon Blanc

**Color:** white · **Body:** light-medium · **Acidity:** high · **Oak affinity:** low (rarely oaked)
**Signature flavors:** grass, gooseberry, green fruits, passionfruit (New Zealand), flint (Loire); piercingly aromatic, razor-sharp
**Home base:** Loire Valley (Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé) — and, as a second home, Marlborough, New Zealand, which made it a global phenomenon.
**Also thrives in:** Chile, South Africa, Bordeaux (traditionally blended with Sémillon for dry and sweet whites), cooler California.
**Character:** Instantly recognizable, extremely refreshing, and best drunk young — one of the few major grapes where bottle age rarely helps. Vigorous in the vineyard; grown too warm it loses its signature aromatics. In Bordeaux it partners Sémillon in both dry whites and the great botrytized sweet wines of Sauternes.
**Ageing potential:** Drink within 1–3 years; top Loire examples can stretch to 5–8.
**Serve at:** 7–10°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants something zesty and aromatic; goat cheese, oysters, salads, or herb-driven dishes are involved; or they ask for "a crisp white."

Riesling

**Color:** white · **Body:** light · **Acidity:** very high · **Oak affinity:** none (rarely oaked)
**Signature flavors:** lime, green apple, white flowers, honey with age, and a distinctive petrol/kerosene note in mature examples; can be bone-dry to lusciously sweet
**Home base:** Germany (Mosel, Rheingau) and Alsace; also noble in Austria.
**Also thrives in:** Australia (Clare and Eden Valleys), New York's Finger Lakes, Michigan, and Ontario — Niagara Riesling is a Canadian calling card, including icewine.
**Character:** The world's most expressive and ageworthy white grape: Riesling is to whites what Cabernet is to reds. It transmits site with precision, ages magnificently for decades on its acidity, and spans every sweetness level — a labeling complexity that's also its marketing curse. Long underpriced relative to quality. Mispronounced constantly; it's "REES-ling."
**Ageing potential:** Exceptional — quality examples 10–30+ years; sweet botrytized and icewine versions even longer.
**Serve at:** 7–10°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a white for spicy food (off-dry Riesling is the classic answer), a high-acid wine for rich dishes, an ageworthy white, or anything icewine-related.

Pinot Gris / Pinot Grigio

**Color:** white (pink-skinned) · **Body:** varies — light (Grigio) to full (Gris) · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** pear, apple, honey and smoke in Alsatian style; neutral citrus in light Italian style; full, golden, and pungent at its best
**Home base:** Alsace, where it counts among the noble grapes; Italy made "Grigio" a global export second only to Prosecco.
**Also thrives in:** Oregon, New Zealand, Australia, Ontario and British Columbia.
**Character:** One pink-skinned grape, two style poles: "Grigio" signals early-picked, light, and crisp; "Gris" signals riper, richer, sometimes off-dry. It is a color mutation cousin of Pinot Noir and can produce anything from characterful to decidedly dull dry whites — producer matters more than usual here.
**Ageing potential:** Most within 1–3 years; rich Alsace examples 5–10.
**Serve at:** 8–11°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants an easy, food-neutral white (Grigio style) or a richer white for pork, smoked fish, or Alsatian dishes (Gris style).

Chenin Blanc

**Color:** white · **Body:** medium · **Acidity:** high · **Oak affinity:** moderate
**Signature flavors:** honey, damp straw, baked apple, quince, lanolin; extremely versatile across sweetness levels
**Home base:** Middle Loire (Vouvray, Savennières, Saumur) — dry, off-dry, sweet, and sparkling.
**Also thrives in:** South Africa, where it's the most planted grape (traditionally "Steen") and old bushvines make some of the world's great-value whites.
**Character:** Perhaps the most underrated major white grape. Its high acidity lets it make nervy, ageworthy wines at every stage of sweetness — botrytized Vouvray can live half a century — plus characterful sparkling Saumur and Vouvray. Cape Chenin from old vines has become a serious international category in its own right.
**Ageing potential:** Top dry and sweet Loire examples 10–40 years; everyday bottles 2–5.
**Serve at:** 8–11°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a white with texture and acidity; pork, roast poultry, or richer seafood; a sparkling alternative to champagne; or a great-value white (South Africa).

Sémillon

**Color:** white · **Body:** full · **Acidity:** medium (low in warm climates)
**Signature flavors:** fig, citrus, lanolin, beeswax; toast and honey with age
**Home base:** Bordeaux — the backbone of Sauternes and Barsac (blended roughly 4:1 with Sauvignon Blanc) and of fine dry Pessac-Léognan whites.
**Also thrives in:** Australia's Hunter Valley, where early-picked, unoaked Semillon starts austere and ages into a long-lived, complex, toasty marvel at barely 11% alcohol.
**Character:** Thin skins make Sémillon exceptionally susceptible to botrytis — a flaw turned virtue in Sauternes, where noble rot concentrates the grapes into golden, honeyed sweet wine. Hunter Semillon is one of wine's great sleeper categories: unimpressive young, remarkable at ten years.
**Ageing potential:** Sauternes 20–50+ years; Hunter Semillon 10–25.
**Serve at:** 8–10°C dry; 6–8°C sweet.
**Recommend when:** the user asks about dessert wine, foie gras, or blue cheese (Sauternes); or wants a distinctive, ageworthy dry white off the beaten path.

Muscat Blanc / Moscato Bianco

**Color:** white · **Body:** light · **Acidity:** medium
**Signature flavors:** grape (the only major variety that actually smells of grapes), orange blossom, musk; usually sweet, often fizzy
**Home base:** Piedmont as Moscato d'Asti; southern France, Corsica, and Greece for sweet fortified styles; Tokaj as Sárga Muskotály.
**Character:** The finest member of the sprawling Muscat family, distinguished by its small round berries (petits grains). Simple pleasures done well: gently sparkling, low-alcohol Moscato d'Asti; golden fortified Muscats in the south of France; Australia's sticky, dark Rutherglen Muscats from a brown-skinned variant. The lesser Muscat of Alexandria mostly makes table grapes and simpler sweet wine.
**Ageing potential:** Drink fizzy styles young; fortified styles keep for decades.
**Serve at:** 6–8°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a low-alcohol sweet sparkler, a brunch wine, a match for fruit desserts, or an introduction to dessert wine.

Gewürztraminer

**Color:** white (pink-skinned) · **Body:** full · **Acidity:** low
**Signature flavors:** lychee, rose petal, ginger, baking spice; deeply aromatic, golden, often off-dry
**Home base:** Alsace, where it's a noble grape; also strong in Alto Adige (its likely birthplace, Tramin) and Ontario/BC.
**Character:** The most operatic of aromatic whites — unmistakable from a meter away. Low acidity and high alcohol demand careful sites and picking decisions; the best balance opulence with freshness. A polarizing grape people tend to love or dismiss, and a legitimately great match for aromatic cuisines.
**Ageing potential:** Most 2–5 years; late-harvest Alsace versions 10–20.
**Serve at:** 8–11°C.
**Recommend when:** the user is eating Thai, Indian, Sichuan, or Alsatian food (Munster cheese, choucroute); or wants the most perfumed white possible.

Viognier

**Color:** white · **Body:** full · **Acidity:** low-medium
**Signature flavors:** apricot, honeysuckle, ginger; oily texture, heady perfume
**Home base:** Condrieu in the northern Rhône — nearly extinct there in the 1960s, since revived worldwide.
**Character:** A rich, aromatic white that walks a tightrope: picked too early it's mute, too late it's blowsy and alcoholic. Traditionally co-fermented in small amounts with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie to stabilize color and add perfume. One of the rare fine whites best drunk young — Condrieu is an exception to the rule that expensive wine should be aged.
**Ageing potential:** Mostly 1–4 years.
**Serve at:** 9–12°C.
**Recommend when:** the user wants a lush, aromatic white with weight; roast chicken, crab, or mildly spiced dishes; or an alternative to oaked Chardonnay.

Albariño / Alvarinho

**Color:** white · **Body:** light-medium · **Acidity:** high
**Signature flavors:** white peach, citrus zest, saline sea-spray note
**Home base:** Rías Baixas in Galicia, northwest Spain, and Vinho Verde country across the border in Portugal.
**Character:** The Atlantic coast in a glass: thick-skinned enough to shrug off Galicia's rain, naturally crisp, and built for seafood. Its rise from regional curiosity to international by-the-glass staple is one of the great modern success stories for indigenous grapes.
**Ageing potential:** Mostly 1–4 years; lees-aged examples longer.
**Serve at:** 7–10°C.
**Recommend when:** the user is eating shellfish, ceviche, or anything maritime; or wants a crisp white that isn't Sauvignon Blanc.

Widely planted but rarely fine

Some of the world's most planted grapes matter more for volume than quality, and the sommelier should recognize them without over-recommending them: Airén (La Mancha; mostly distilled for brandy), Trebbiano Toscano / Ugni Blanc (neutral; the base of Cognac), Carignan (harsh when overcropped, though old vines in Priorat and the Languedoc can be excellent), Bobal (sturdy Spanish reds), Rkatsiteli (high-acid Eastern European workhorse), Macabeo/Viura (Rioja and Cava whites), and Graševina/Welschriesling (underrated in Croatia — no relation to true Riesling).

Notable parentages (useful trivia and recommendation logic)

- Cabernet Sauvignon = Cabernet Franc × Sauvignon Blanc.
- Chardonnay, Gamay, Aligoté, Melon de Bourgogne, and Auxerrois all descend from Pinot Noir × Gouais Blanc.
- Merlot is closely related to Malbec (Côt); Pinot appears to be a great-grandparent of Syrah.
- Zinfandel = Primitivo = Croatia's Tribidrag.
- Practical use: a user who loves one member of a family is a good candidate for its relatives.

Canadian context (TC-Cellar home turf)

- Riesling and Chardonnay lead Ontario whites; Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, and Gamay lead the reds — all cool-climate specialists.
- Icewine (Riesling, Vidal, Cabernet Franc) is Canada's signature category.
- British Columbia's Okanagan Valley, a semi-desert, ripens fuller styles including Syrah and Bordeaux varieties.

Phenolics — the family that shapes red wine

Phenolic compounds (polyphenols) are the group responsible for a red wine's color, tannin, structure, bitterness, and much of its ageability. They come mostly from grape skins, seeds, and stems, which is why red winemaking (fermenting on skins) extracts far more phenolics than white winemaking (pressing before fermentation).

The two headline categories are anthocyanins (pigments — color) and tannins (structure and astringency). Both are far more concentrated in red grapes and in thick-skinned varieties, and both are central to why some wines age for decades and others don't.

Why it matters to tasting: phenolics are what you feel as much as taste — the grip, the drying sensation, the weight. A pale, low-tannin wine and a dense, gripping one differ mostly in phenolic content and extraction.

data.content:
Anthocyanins — where red color comes from

Anthocyanins are the pigments in dark grape skins that give red wine its color. The pulp of almost all wine grapes is greyish-clear; color comes from skin contact during fermentation, which is why:
- Red wine ferments on its skins.
- White wine is pressed off the skins before fermentation.
- Rosé takes a short skin contact, then presses off — tinting the juice pink.
- "Teinturier" grapes are the rare exception with red-fleshed pulp.

Anthocyanin color is pH-sensitive: brighter, more purple-red at low pH (high acidity); duller and bluer at high pH. Free anthocyanins are unstable on their own — over time they combine with tannins into stable polymeric pigments, which is how a wine keeps color as it ages even as the original pigments fade.

Why it matters to tasting: a young red's purple rim signals fresh anthocyanins and high acidity; a brick-orange rim signals age and the shift to polymerized pigment. Color at the rim is one of the most reliable visual clues to a red's maturity.

data.content:
Tannins — structure, astringency, and age

Tannins are phenolic compounds that bind to proteins — including the proteins in your saliva — which is what produces the drying, grippy sensation of astringency. They come from:
- Grape skins — generally riper, softer, more desirable tannins.
- Grape seeds (pips) — harsher, more bitter; why gentle pressing avoids crushing seeds.
- Stems — green, astringent if unripe; some winemakers use whole-cluster fermentation deliberately for structure and aroma when stems are ripe.
- Oak — barrels contribute their own wood tannins.

Tannins serve as a natural preservative and are the main reason age-worthy reds can improve for decades. Young tannins are firm and sometimes harsh; over time they polymerize (link into larger molecules) and eventually precipitate as sediment, so an old red is both paler and softer than it was in youth.

Managing tannin extraction during fermentation is a core red-winemaking skill — punch-downs, pump-overs, and time on skins all control how much tannin is drawn out and how smooth it ends up.

Why it matters to tasting: high, firm tannin plus deep color usually means a wine built to age. Soft, resolved tannin means it's ready now. Bitter, green tannin suggests underripe fruit or seed/stem extraction.

How tannin ripeness differs from sugar ripeness

A crucial distinction for understanding modern wine: phenolic (tannin) ripeness and sugar ripeness don't always arrive together. In warm climates and with climate change, sugar can race ahead — reaching high potential alcohol — while tannins and flavors lag behind, still green.

This drives the "hang time" dilemma: growers delay picking to let tannins ripen, but the extra time pushes sugar (and therefore alcohol) higher. It's a major reason modern reds have crept up in alcohol. The reverse problem — ripe sugar but unripe tannin — gives high-alcohol wines with harsh, green structure.

Why it matters to tasting: a wine that's both high in alcohol and green/astringent points to a mismatch between sugar and phenolic ripeness at harvest.

Organic acids in the finished wine

The main acids carried from grape to glass:
- Tartaric acid — grape's signature acid, strong and stable, the primary contributor to a wine's low pH and freshness.
- Malic acid — sharper, "green apple"; abundant in underripe/cool-climate fruit, consumed by MLF.
- Lactic acid — milder, "milky"; produced by MLF from malic acid.
- Citric acid — minor.
- Acetic acid — the volatile one; small amounts normal, excess is the vinegar fault (VA).
- Succinic, lactic, and others — produced during fermentation.

Acidity provides freshness, balances sweetness and alcohol, sharpens flavor, and — via low pH — protects color and microbial stability. As a wine ages, perceived acidity can seem to soften even though measured acidity stays roughly constant, because developing complexity distracts from it.
data.section_title: Organic acids in the finished wine

data.content:
Tartrate stability and "wine diamonds"

Tartaric acid combines with potassium to form potassium bitartrate (cream of tartar), which is soluble in warm liquid but precipitates as harmless crystals when wine gets cold. These glassy "wine diamonds" alarm consumers but are a sign of nothing wrong.

To prevent them appearing in bottle, many wines are cold-stabilized — chilled to near freezing (about 0°C) before bottling so the crystals drop out in the tank instead. Alternatives include contact seeding and electrodialysis. Some fine-wine producers skip it, accepting crystals as natural.

Why it matters to tasting: crystals on a cork or at the bottom of a bottle are cosmetic, not a fault — useful for the sommelier to reassure a worried drinker.

Aroma — the three layers

A wine's smell is built in three overlapping layers, and naming them helps a taster place a wine:
- Primary aromas — from the grape itself: fruit, floral, herbal, mineral character. Dominant in young wines.
- Secondary aromas — from winemaking: yeast/lees (bread, brioche), MLF (butter, cream), and oak (vanilla, spice, toast, coconut).
- Tertiary aromas — from ageing: the complex "bouquet" of maturity — dried fruit, nuts, honey, forest floor, leather, savory and earthy notes formed slowly by oxidation and molecular evolution in bottle.

Why it matters to tasting: a wine dominated by primary fruit reads as young; one showing tertiary bouquet reads as mature. Recognizing which layer dominates is central to estimating a wine's age and readiness.

Aroma chemistry — the compound families

The molecules behind those aromas:
- Esters — fruity and floral; formed during fermentation, prominent in young wines, and fading with age. Responsible for much of the "primary fruit" in youthful whites and light reds.
- Higher alcohols (fusel alcohols) — contribute body and, in excess, harsh solvent notes.
- Terpenes — floral and grapey; the signature of aromatic varieties like Muscat, Riesling, and Gewürztraminer.
- Thiols (volatile sulfur compounds) — the passionfruit/gooseberry/grapefruit punch of Sauvignon Blanc; also, in the wrong form, the reductive rotten-egg/struck-match faults.
- Methoxypyrazines — green bell pepper, herbaceous; marker of underripe Cabernet family and Sauvignon Blanc.
- Rotundone — the black-pepper compound, characteristic of Syrah.
- Norisoprenoids — from carotenoid breakdown; contribute to aged/tertiary complexity.
- Aldehydes — notably acetaldehyde, a marker of oxidation (and intentional in sherry).

Why it matters to tasting: these are the vocabulary behind tasting notes — bell pepper (pyrazine), pepper (rotundone), passionfruit (thiol), rose/lychee (terpene). The sommelier can reason backward from a described smell to grape and ripeness.

Why wine ages — the bottle chemistry

Ageing in bottle is driven by slow reactions among phenolics, acids, and the small amount of oxygen dissolved in the wine and held in the headspace under the cork:
- Tannins and pigments polymerize — linking into larger molecules that soften astringency, shift color from purple to brick, and eventually precipitate as sediment.
- Primary fruit fades as esters break down; tertiary bouquet develops through oxidative and other reactions.
- The wine moves toward a harmonious whole at its peak, then eventually declines — losing fruit, with acidity or tannin coming to dominate as harmony breaks down.

Not all wine improves with age — this is a persistent myth. The majority of wine is made to drink young. Ageability depends on having enough tannin, acidity, and concentration to evolve rather than simply fade.

Why it matters to tasting: the sommelier should match ageing advice to structure — high tannin/acid/concentration = candidate for the cellar; light, low-tannin, fruity = drink now.
data.section_title: Why wine ages — the bottle chemistry

data.content:
Ageing potential by style (practical guide)

Approximate windows, all else equal:
- Light, fruity reds (Beaujolais/Gamay, simple Pinot, Dolcetto): drink within 1–4 years.
- Aromatic whites (Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Grigio, most Muscat): 1–3 years, best fresh.
- Mid-weight reds (Merlot, Chianti, Rioja Crianza): 3–8 years.
- Structured reds (Cabernet, Barolo, Northern Rhône, Bordeaux Cru Classé, Barossa Shiraz): 10–30+ years.
- High-acid ageworthy whites (Riesling, Chablis, Chenin, Hunter Semillon): 10–20+ years.
- Great sweet wines (Sauternes, Tokaji, botrytized Riesling, icewine): 20–50+ years.
- Fortified (vintage port longest of all; tawny, sherry, madeira ready on release): variable, vintage port 20–50+.

Half-bottles age faster and magnums slower, because the ratio of headspace oxygen to wine volume differs — a reason collectors pay premiums for large formats.

The dumb phase

Many fine wines pass through an awkward "dumb" or closed stage — often around the point where youthful primary fruit has faded but tertiary complexity hasn't yet emerged, and complex compounds are still forming. White Rhône and top reds are especially prone to it. A wine tasted in this phase can seem mute and disappointing; patience usually rewards.

Why it matters to tasting: the sommelier can reassure a drinker that a closed young wine of good pedigree may simply be in its dumb phase, not flawed.

Clarification and fining

A finished wine is naturally cloudy and must be clarified before bottling:
- Settling and racking — the most natural method: solids sink, clear wine is drawn off the top; repeated over time.
- Fining — adding an agent that binds to suspended particles and drags them down. Traditional fining agents include egg white, gelatin, isinglass (fish), casein (milk), and bentonite (clay); vegan alternatives (pea protein, bentonite alone) are increasingly common. Fining can also soften harsh tannins or remove bitterness.
- Filtration — physically straining the wine through membranes or pads to remove particles and microbes.

The filtration debate: overdone, it can strip flavor and ageing potential; underdone, it leaves the wine prey to microbes and refermentation. Many "natural" wines are unfined and unfiltered, accepting some cloudiness for a fuller expression.

Why it matters to tasting: slight haze or sediment in a natural/unfiltered wine is stylistic, not necessarily a fault; fined-and-filtered wines are bright and stable but some argue less texturally complete.

Stabilization — keeping wine sound in bottle

Before bottling, wine must be made stable so it doesn't throw deposits, haze, refermentation, or spoilage later:
- Tartrate stability — cold stabilization (above) to precipitate bitartrate crystals in advance.
- Protein stability (whites) — unstable grape proteins can form haze if the wine warms; bentonite fining removes them.
- Microbial stability — ensuring no fermentable sugar plus live yeast/bacteria remain that could referment; achieved through fermenting dry, sterile filtration, and adequate SO₂.
- Oxidative stability — sufficient free SO₂ and good closures to prevent browning.

Why it matters to tasting: most faults a consumer encounters (haze, refermentation fizz, browning) trace back to a stabilization step skipped or a closure that let in oxygen.
data.section_title: Stabilization — keeping wine sound in bottle

data.content:
The main wine faults (recognition guide)

- Cork taint (TCA) — musty wet-cardboard/damp-basement smell, mutes fruit; caused by the compound trichloroanisole, usually from cork. Not harmful, but ruins the wine.
- Oxidation — bruised apple, sherry-like, flat; browning color. From excess oxygen or a failed seal.
- Volatile acidity (VA) — vinegar and/or nail-polish (ethyl acetate); from acetic acid bacteria.
- Reduction — rotten egg, struck match, boiled cabbage, garlic; from volatile sulfur compounds, often in low-oxygen (screwcap) conditions. Frequently blows off with air or a decant.
- Brettanomyces ("Brett") — barnyard, band-aid, smoky, horsey; a spoilage yeast. Divisive: a fault in excess, "complexity" to some in small doses.
- Heat damage (maderization) — cooked, stewed, flat; from storage too warm.
- Light strike — cabbage/wet-wool notes in wines (especially sparkling and in clear bottles) exposed to light.

Why it matters to tasting: distinguishing a genuine fault from a stylistic choice (natural-wine VA/Brett, reductive struck-match) is one of the most useful things a sommelier does. Reduction often clears with air; TCA never does.

From chemistry to the glass — summary

1. Phenolics (anthocyanins + tannins) set a red's color, structure, and ageability; extraction during fermentation controls how much ends up in the wine.
2. Acids and pH govern freshness, stability, and color; tartrates precipitate harmlessly in the cold.
3. Aroma builds in three layers — primary (grape), secondary (winemaking), tertiary (age) — from identifiable compound families.
4. Ageing is slow polymerization and oxidation: tannins soften, color shifts, fruit fades, bouquet develops, then harmony eventually breaks.
5. Clarification, fining, and stabilization make the wine bright and sound; skipping steps (by choice or error) explains most deposits and faults a drinker meets.
data.section_title: From chemistry to the glass — summary

data.content:
Alcoholic fermentation — the core reaction

Alcoholic fermentation is the conversion of grape sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide by yeast, with heat released as a byproduct. In simple terms: glucose and fructose (the two grape sugars) are metabolized, roughly 17 grams of sugar per liter yielding about 1% alcohol by volume. A must at 220 g/L of sugar therefore produces a wine near 13% alcohol.

Fermentation also generates hundreds of secondary compounds — glycerol, higher alcohols, esters, aldehydes, and organic acids — that shape a wine's texture and aroma far beyond mere ethanol. The reaction is anaerobic in its main phase: yeast ferments sugar in the absence of oxygen, though a small amount of oxygen early on helps yeast build healthy cell membranes.

Why it matters to tasting: the completeness of fermentation determines dryness. If yeast converts all the sugar, the wine is dry; if fermentation stops early (naturally or by intervention), residual sugar remains and the wine is off-dry or sweet.

Wine yeasts — Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the others

The dominant wine yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, prized because it tolerates high alcohol, ferments reliably to dryness, and produces clean flavors. It is present naturally on grape skins and cellar surfaces, but most modern wineries inoculate with selected cultured strains for predictability.

Before Saccharomyces takes over, non-Saccharomyces "wild" yeasts (genera such as Hanseniaspora/Kloeckera, Candida, Metschnikowia, Torulaspora) dominate the early hours. These are less alcohol-tolerant and die off as ethanol rises, but they contribute aromatic complexity — which is part of why spontaneous (wild) ferments taste different from inoculated ones.

Cultured vs. ambient yeast — the stylistic debate:
- Cultured yeast behaves predictably, ferments cleanly, and can be chosen to emphasize particular aromas or to handle difficult conditions (high sugar, low nutrients, sparkling base wine).
- Ambient/indigenous yeast is less predictable but, its advocates argue, adds interest and a sense of place — arguably an aspect of terroir.
- Practically, a strong strain established in one vat will often kick-start neighbors.
data.section_title: Wine yeasts — Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the others

data.content:
Yeast nutrition and stuck fermentation

Yeast needs more than sugar: it requires nitrogen (as ammonium and amino acids — measured as YAN, yeast assimilable nitrogen), plus vitamins, minerals, and survival factors. When nitrogen is deficient, fermentation slows or halts.

A stuck fermentation — where sugar remains but yeast activity has stopped — is the winemaker's nightmare, because a sweet, low-alcohol, partially fermented liquid is highly vulnerable to spoilage microbes. Causes include nitrogen deficiency, excessive temperature, very high initial sugar, toxic levels of ethanol, and inhibition by excess SO₂.

Why it matters to tasting: a well-nourished, clean fermentation gives fresh, fruity, fault-free wine. Nutrient stress can throw off reductive (sulfurous, struck-match, rotten-egg) aromas from hydrogen sulfide production.

Fermentation temperature and its effect on style

Temperature is one of the winemaker's most powerful levers:
- Cool fermentation (12–17°C) for aromatic whites preserves delicate, fruity, floral esters. Too cool and fermentation is sluggish.
- Warm fermentation (20–32°C) for reds extracts more color, tannin, and flavor from the skins, and produces fuller-bodied, more structured wines.
- Fermentation is exothermic — it generates heat — so vats naturally warm up and often need cooling. Too hot (above ~35°C) and fermentation can "boil off" volatile aromatics or even kill the yeast, causing a stuck ferment.

Rule of thumb for the sommelier: bright, primary-fruit whites imply cool ferments; deeply colored, structured reds imply warmer ones.
data.section_title: Fermentation temperature and its effect on style

data.content:
Malolactic conversion (MLF) — the second fermentation

Malolactic conversion (also called malolactic fermentation, though it's bacterial not yeast-driven) is carried out by lactic acid bacteria, chiefly Oenococcus oeni. It converts harsh malic acid (the sharp acid of green apples) into softer lactic acid (the mild acid of milk), releasing CO₂.

Effects:
- Lowers total acidity and raises pH, making the wine rounder and less tart.
- Adds texture and flavor — the buttery, creamy note in many Chardonnays comes from diacetyl, a byproduct of MLF.
- Microbial stability — once malic acid is consumed, it can't be fermented later in bottle, avoiding unwanted fizz and haze.

Where it's used:
- Nearly all red wines go through MLF — it softens them and adds complexity.
- Most premium Chardonnay (including white Burgundy) is encouraged through MLF for texture.
- Aromatic, high-acid whites (Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc) are usually blocked from MLF — by cool temperatures, SO₂ additions, or filtering out the bacteria — to keep them crisp and preserve fruit.

Why it matters to tasting: buttery, creamy, "milky" texture in a white signals MLF; racy, tart, green-apple freshness signals it was suppressed.

Lactic acid bacteria as spoilage agents

The same family of lactic acid bacteria that performs beneficial MLF can spoil wine under the wrong conditions. If they act on sugars rather than malic acid — for instance in a stuck ferment with residual sugar, or at high pH with low SO₂ — they can produce:
- Volatile acidity (excess acetic acid — vinegar).
- Mousiness — an off-flavor perceptible on the finish, associated with certain bacteria.
- Biogenic amines and other off-compounds.

Control relies on completing fermentation cleanly, maintaining adequate SO₂, managing pH, and hygiene.
data.section_title: Lactic acid bacteria as spoilage agents

data.content:
Acetic acid bacteria and volatile acidity

Acetic acid bacteria (Acetobacter, Gluconobacter) require oxygen and convert ethanol into acetic acid (vinegar) and ethyl acetate (nail-polish-remover smell). Together these make up much of a wine's volatile acidity (VA).

Small amounts of VA can add lift and complexity; excess is a fault. The main defenses are limiting oxygen exposure (keeping barrels topped up, tanks full, sound closures) and maintaining protective SO₂. Wines most at risk are those left with air contact, in ullaged barrels, or with high pH and low sulfur.

Why it matters to tasting: a sharp vinegar or solvent note on the nose is VA. Natural wines made with minimal SO₂ sometimes show elevated VA, which is why the style can be polarizing.
data.section_title: Acetic acid bacteria and volatile acidity

data.content:
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) — the winemaker's essential tool

Sulfur dioxide is the most important additive in winemaking, valued for three properties:
1. Antimicrobial — inhibits unwanted yeasts and bacteria (spoilage organisms, and it can be used to block MLF).
2. Antioxidant — protects against oxidation that browns the wine and dulls fruit.
3. Antioxidasic — deactivates oxidative enzymes from the grape (especially important with rot-affected fruit).

SO₂ exists in wine in free and bound forms; only free SO₂ (particularly molecular SO₂, which depends on pH) is protective. Lower-pH wines need less SO₂ to stay protected, which is one reason high-acid wines are more stable.

Regulations cap total SO₂, and "contains sulfites" must be declared on labels because a minority of people are sensitive. "Natural" and low-intervention winemaking minimizes SO₂, trading some stability for a particular expression — and accepting higher spoilage risk.

Why it matters to tasting: freshly bottled or heavily sulfured wine can show a struck-match or matchstick note that blows off with air. Under-sulfured wine is more prone to oxidation (bruised-apple, sherry-like notes) and VA.
data.section_title: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) — the winemakers essential tool

data.content:
Oxygen — friend and enemy

Oxygen's role flips depending on stage:
- Early (fermentation): a little oxygen helps yeast build healthy membranes and ferment strongly.
- Ageing (controlled): slow, tiny oxygen ingress through barrels or via deliberate micro-oxygenation softens tannins and stabilizes color in reds.
- Excess/uncontrolled: oxygen browns wine, fades fruit, and feeds acetic acid bacteria.

Protective vs. oxidative white winemaking is a key stylistic fork:
- Protective (reductive): juice is shielded from oxygen with SO₂ and cool temperatures to preserve fresh primary fruit — standard for Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, aromatic whites.
- Oxidative: grapes and juice are deliberately exposed to some oxygen early, pre-empting later oxidation and building secondary, more complex flavors — traditional for top Chardonnay and white Burgundy.

Must composition — what's in grape juice

Grape must (unfermented juice) is roughly 70–80% water, plus:
- Sugars — glucose and fructose, in near-equal amounts at ripeness; the raw material for alcohol.
- Acids — mainly tartaric (grape's signature acid, stable and strong) and malic (sharper, decreases as grapes ripen); small amounts of citric.
- Phenolics — tannins and pigments, concentrated in skins and seeds.
- Nitrogen compounds — amino acids and ammonium, the yeast's nitrogen supply.
- Minerals — potassium, calcium, magnesium.
- Aroma precursors — often flavorless in the grape, released as aroma during fermentation and ageing.

Sugar accumulates and acid falls as grapes ripen — the central tension of harvest timing. Pick too early and the wine is thin and tart; too late and it's high in alcohol and flabby.
data.section_title: Must composition — whats in grape juice

data.content:
Acidity, pH, and why they're different

- Total (titratable) acidity measures the concentration of acids — how sour the wine tastes.
- pH measures acid strength/activity on a logarithmic scale — and it governs microbial stability, SO₂ effectiveness, and color.
- Low pH (high acidity) wines are fresher-tasting, more microbially stable, need less SO₂, and hold brighter red color. High pH wines are rounder but more fragile and prone to spoilage and browning.

Warm-climate grapes often have high sugar but low acidity and high pH — which is why winemakers in hot regions routinely acidify with tartaric acid. Cool-climate grapes may need the opposite (deacidification, or MLF to soften).
data.section_title: Acidity, pH, and why theyre different

data.content:
Chaptalization and enrichment

Chaptalization is adding sugar to the fermenting must to raise the final alcohol (not sweetness — the added sugar ferments out). Named for Napoleon's minister Jean-Antoine Chaptal, it's a centuries-old practice in cool regions where grapes struggle to reach full ripeness. AOC rules typically cap the boost at around 2% alcohol. Warmer vintages and better viticulture have steadily reduced the need for it.

Concentration and alcohol adjustment

Modern cellars can adjust must and wine mechanically:
- Concentration (reverse osmosis, vacuum evaporation, cryoextraction) removes water to intensify sugar/flavor.
- Alcohol reduction (reverse osmosis, spinning cone, low-temperature distillation) trims excess alcohol in wines that fermented too hot — a growing concern in warm regions and with climate change.
- Saignée ("bleeding" off a portion of juice early in a red ferment) increases the skin-to-juice ratio, concentrating color and tannin in what remains — and yields rosé as a byproduct.

Why it matters to tasting: these tools explain why a wine from a hot vintage can still be balanced, and why alcohol levels have crept up over recent decades.

The fermentation-to-glass summary

1. Ripe grapes supply sugar, acid, phenolics, and aroma precursors.
2. Yeast (wild then Saccharomyces) ferments sugar to alcohol, CO₂, heat, and hundreds of flavor compounds; temperature controls style.
3. Lactic acid bacteria may perform MLF, softening acidity and adding creamy texture.
4. SO₂ and oxygen management protect the wine and steer it between fresh/reductive and complex/oxidative styles.
5. Acidity, pH, and any adjustments (chaptalization, acidification, concentration) set the final balance the taster perceives.

Alsace — overview

Alsace sits in northeastern France, along the German border, sheltered from Atlantic rain by the Vosges mountains — which makes it one of France's driest, sunniest wine regions despite its northern latitude. Its history has shifted between France and Germany, and its wine culture reflects both: German grape varieties and a focus on aromatic whites, but a French dry style. Alsace is unusual in France for labeling wines by grape variety, and for its tall, flute-shaped bottles. It is overwhelmingly a white-wine region.
Recommend when: the user wants aromatic, expressive dry whites; a match for spicy or aromatic cuisine; or varietally labeled French wine.

The noble grapes of Alsace

Four grapes are designated "noble" in Alsace and may be used for its top wines:
- Riesling — the most prized; dry, racy, mineral, citrus and stone-fruit, highly ageworthy. Alsace Riesling is typically drier and fuller than German.
- Gewurztraminer (spelled without the umlaut in Alsace) — intensely aromatic; lychee, rose, ginger, spice; full-bodied, low-acid, often faintly off-dry.
- Pinot Gris — rich, full, smoky, honeyed; more powerful than Italian Pinot Grigio.
- Muscat — dry, grapey, floral; a distinctive aromatic apéritif style.
Recommend when: matching aromatics and food — Riesling for minerality, Gewurztraminer for perfume and spice-food, Pinot Gris for richness, Muscat as a dry aromatic apéritif.

Other Alsace grapes

- Pinot Blanc (and Auxerrois) — soft, gentle, easy dry whites; also the base of much Crémant.
- Sylvaner — light, crisp, earthy; a traditional everyday white.
- Pinot Noir — the only red permitted; historically light, but increasingly serious and structured as the climate warms.
Recommend when: the user wants an easy, gentle white (Pinot Blanc), a crisp everyday white (Sylvaner), or a cool-climate Pinot Noir.

Dryness in Alsace — a labeling note

Alsace can be confusing on sweetness: most basic wines are dry, but Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer especially can carry noticeable residual sugar without saying so on the label. Producers increasingly indicate a dryness scale. The key point for the sommelier: Riesling and Muscat are usually dry; Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer may be off-dry depending on producer and ripeness.
Recommend when: the user is unsure whether an Alsace wine will be sweet, or wants a guaranteed-dry aromatic white.
data.section_title: Dryness in Alsace — a labeling note

data.content:
Alsace Grand Cru

Alsace has 51 Grand Cru vineyards — specific, delimited sites recognized for superior terroir, generally planted to the four noble grapes. A Grand Cru on the label signals a single top vineyard and usually a more concentrated, mineral, ageworthy wine. The rest of the region's wine is labeled simply "Alsace AOC," often with the grape variety.
Recommend when: the user wants a step up in concentration and terroir expression, or an ageworthy Alsace white.

Sweet Alsace — Vendanges Tardives & SGN

Alsace makes two levels of naturally sweet wine from ripe or botrytis-affected noble grapes:
- Vendanges Tardives (VT) — "late harvest"; rich, concentrated, off-dry to sweet.
- Sélection de Grains Nobles (SGN) — "selection of noble berries"; intensely sweet, botrytized, rare and long-lived.
Both are made from Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, or Muscat.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a rich late-harvest or botrytized dessert wine, or a match for foie gras and rich desserts.

Crémant dAlsace

Alsace is one of France's largest producers of Crémant — traditional-method sparkling wine, most often based on Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, sometimes Pinot Noir (for rosé), Chardonnay, or Riesling. Crisp, fresh, and excellent value, it's a serious Champagne alternative.
Serve at: 8°C.
Recommend when: the user wants an affordable, high-quality sparkling wine.

Food pairing — Alsaces strength

Alsace's aromatic, often dry-but-fruity whites are among the most food-versatile wines in the world, and a classic answer to cuisines that trouble other wines: Gewurztraminer with Munster cheese, Thai, Indian, or Sichuan food; Riesling with choucroute (sauerkraut with sausages), trout, or pork; Pinot Gris with smoked fish or richer poultry.
Recommend when: the user is eating spicy, aromatic, or Alsatian food and needs a versatile wine.

Quick regional summary

- What: dry, sunny northeast France; aromatic white-wine region, varietally labeled, tall flute bottles.
- Noble grapes: Riesling (mineral, dry, ageworthy), Gewurztraminer (perfumed, spice-food), Pinot Gris (rich, smoky), Muscat (dry, grapey).
- Also: Pinot Blanc/Sylvaner (easy whites), Pinot Noir (the lone red), Crémant dAlsace (sparkling).
- Sweet: Vendanges Tardives and Sélection de Grains Nobles.
- Strength: unbeatable with spicy and aromatic cuisines.

China

China is now one of the world's largest vineyard holders and a significant, fast-evolving wine producer. Quality wine has advanced rapidly this century, moving from underripe early efforts to genuinely accomplished reds. The standout region is Ningxia (on the arid, high plains near the Helan Mountains), making structured, ambitious Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends that have won international acclaim. Other regions include Shandong (coastal, humid), Xinjiang (far west, continental), and Yunnan (high-altitude south). In much of the north, winters are so severe that vines must be buried each autumn and uncovered each spring. Marselan (a Cabernet-Grenache crossing) is emerging as a distinctive Chinese signature red.
Recommend when: the user is curious about Chinese wine, wants an ambitious Ningxia Cabernet/Bordeaux blend, or asks about Marselan.

Japan

Japan's signature is Koshu — a pale-pink-skinned indigenous grape making delicate, subtle, low-alcohol, mineral dry whites with citrus and a gentle character, a natural match for Japanese cuisine (sushi, sashimi). The main region is Yamanashi, near Mount Fuji. Japan's humid, rainy climate makes viticulture challenging (vines are often trained high on pergolas for airflow), but quality Koshu and Japanese-grown international varieties (including the red hybrid Muscat Bailey A) are gaining recognition. Note: much cheap "Japanese wine" is actually made from imported bulk — genuine domestic wine (Nihon wine) is a defined, higher category.
Recommend when: the user wants a delicate, food-friendly white for Japanese food, or is curious about Koshu.

India

India has a small but growing wine industry, concentrated in cooler, higher-elevation areas like Nashik (Maharashtra) and around Bangalore. Producers make international-variety wines (Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Shiraz, Cabernet) and traditional-method sparkling, geared to a rising domestic market. A hot climate and monsoon make timing and site selection critical.
Recommend when: the user asks about Indian wine or an emerging-market option.

England

England (and Wales) has become a genuine cool-climate success story, driven by climate change and chalk soils. Its strength is traditional-method sparkling wine — made from the Champagne grapes (Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Meunier) on the same chalk geology that runs under Champagne, in the South Downs (Sussex, Hampshire, Kent). English sparkling is crisp, high-acid, and increasingly acclaimed, rivalling Champagne in blind tastings. Still wines (aromatic whites, Pinot Noir) are improving as the climate warms.
Serve at: 8°C sparkling.
Recommend when: the user wants a high-quality cool-climate sparkling wine, or a Champagne alternative from an unexpected place.

Quick summary asia

- China: large and fast-rising; Ningxia (ambitious Cabernet/Bordeaux blends), emerging Marselan; vines buried in cold-winter north.
- Japan: delicate indigenous Koshu white (Yamanashi); food-friendly, subtle; challenging humid climate.
- India: small, growing; international grapes and sparkling around Nashik.
- England: cool-climate chalk-soil traditional-method sparkling (Champagne grapes), a genuine rising star.

Australia — overview

Australia is a major wine power spanning a huge range of climates, from hot inland zones making value wine to cool, elevated, and maritime sites making world-class fine wine. It's labeled by grape variety, with origin shown by GI (Geographical Indication) regions. Australia's flagship is Shiraz (Syrah), but it also excels at Cabernet, Chardonnay, Riesling, and increasingly cool-climate and alternative varieties. A long-running move toward freshness, elegance, and cooler sites has reshaped the modern Australian style.
Recommend when: the user wants bold, ripe reds (Shiraz), or — increasingly — elegant, cool-climate Australian wines.

Shiraz — the flagship

Shiraz (the same grape as Syrah) is Australia's signature red, in two broad styles: the rich, powerful, warm-climate version (Barossa, McLaren Vale) — dense, dark-fruited, chocolatey, sometimes with a hint of pepper — and the cooler, more peppery, savory, elegant version (Victoria, cool hills). Often blended with Grenache and Mourvèdre (GSM) or, distinctively, co-fermented with a little Viognier.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a bold, ripe, generous red (warm-climate Shiraz) or a savory, peppery, elegant one (cool-climate Shiraz).

Barossa Valley & South Australias warm regions

South Australia is the country's wine engine. Its warm regions make Australia's most famous rich reds:
- Barossa Valley — the icon; powerful, opulent Shiraz (including ancient pre-phylloxera old-vine vineyards) and rich Grenache and Cabernet.
- McLaren Vale — maritime-warm; plush Shiraz and Grenache, Mediterranean varieties.
- Clare Valley and Eden Valley — higher, cooler pockets famous for bone-dry, lime-scented, ageworthy Riesling (a benchmark), plus fine Shiraz.
Recommend when: the user wants powerful Barossa Shiraz, plush McLaren Vale reds, or Australia's benchmark dry Riesling (Clare/Eden).

data.content:
Coonawarra & Cabernet

Coonawarra, in South Australia, is famous for its terra rossa (red soil over limestone) and is Australia's benchmark region for Cabernet Sauvignon — structured, blackcurrant-and-mint-scented, ageworthy. Margaret River (see below) is the other great Cabernet region.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a structured, ageworthy Australian Cabernet with a distinctive minty/eucalypt lift.

Margaret River (Western Australia)

Margaret River, on the far southwest coast, is a maritime, moderate region making some of Australia's most refined wines: elegant Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet-Merlot blends (Bordeaux-like), and superb Chardonnay (among the country's best), plus a distinctive Sauvignon Blanc–Semillon (SSB) white blend. Higher-end and quality-focused.
Recommend when: the user wants a refined, Bordeaux-style Australian Cabernet or a top Australian Chardonnay.

Victoria — cool-climate diversity

Victoria has the most diverse wine scene, largely cooler and more elegant:
- Yarra Valley — cool; elegant Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and peppery Shiraz; sparkling.
- Mornington Peninsula — cool, maritime; refined Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
- Heathcote — distinctive rich Shiraz on ancient red soils.
- Rutherglen — hot; famous for lusciously sweet fortified Muscat and Topaque (Muscadelle) — dark, sticky, treacle-and-raisin dessert wines of world renown.
- Geelong, Beechworth, King Valley (the last known for Italian varieties like Prosecco/Glera).
Recommend when: the user wants cool-climate Australian Pinot/Chardonnay (Yarra, Mornington), or a legendary sweet fortified (Rutherglen Muscat).

Other regions & Semillon

- New South Wales — Hunter Valley — hot and humid, yet famous for a unique, ageless, low-alcohol dry Semillon that ages into a toasty marvel, plus earthy Shiraz.
- Tasmania — cool, island climate; premier sparkling wine (traditional method), plus excellent Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Riesling; a rising star as the mainland warms.
- Riverland/Riverina — hot, irrigated inland; the source of much value/bulk wine (and botrytized sweet Semillon in the Riverina).
Recommend when: the user wants ageworthy Hunter Semillon, or cool-climate Tasmanian sparkling and Pinot.

Quick regional summary australia

- Australia: labeled by grape; origins via GI. Flagship Shiraz (rich warm-climate vs peppery cool-climate).
- South Australia: Barossa (opulent Shiraz, old vines), McLaren Vale (plush reds), Clare/Eden (benchmark dry Riesling), Coonawarra (terra rossa Cabernet).
- Western Australia: Margaret River (refined Cabernet & Chardonnay).
- Victoria: cool & diverse — Yarra/Mornington (Pinot/Chardonnay), Rutherglen (sweet fortified Muscat).
- New South Wales: Hunter Valley (ageless Semillon). Tasmania: top sparkling & Pinot.

Beaujolais — overview

Beaujolais lies just south of Burgundy, on granite and schist hills, and makes light, juicy, low-tannin red wine from the Gamay grape. It is famous for a joyful, gulpable style — often made by carbonic maceration (whole-berry fermentation), which emphasizes bright fruit and reduces tannin. Beaujolais ranges from simple, cheerful bottles to serious, terroir-driven crus that rival village Burgundy at a fraction of the price. It is a cornerstone of the natural-wine movement.
Recommend when: the user wants a light, chillable, low-tannin red; a versatile food or apéritif red; or a value alternative to Pinot Noir.

Beaujolais quality tiers

- Beaujolais Nouveau — released the third Thursday of November, weeks after harvest; ultra-fresh, fruity (sometimes banana/bubblegum from carbonic maceration), meant to be drunk immediately. A marketing phenomenon more than a serious wine.
- Beaujolais / Beaujolais-Villages — everyday, fruity, easy reds; Villages a step up.
- The ten Crus — the top tier, named villages that don't use "Beaujolais" on the label: Morgon (structured, dark-fruited, ageworthy), Moulin-à-Vent ("the king," firmest and most Burgundian), Fleurie (floral, silky), Brouilly and Côte de Brouilly (fruity, largest), plus Chénas, Chiroubles, Juliénas, Régnié, Saint-Amour. Cru Beaujolais can age 3–10 years.
Serve at: 12–14°C — genuinely chillable.
Recommend when: matching seriousness — Nouveau for a party, Villages for everyday, crus (Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie) for a real wine that over-delivers on value.

Provence — the rosé heartland

Provence, in the sunny Mediterranean southeast, is the world's benchmark for dry rosé — pale, crisp, and elegant, with delicate red-fruit, citrus, and herb notes. Rosé is roughly 90% of production. Made mainly from Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, and Mourvèdre, Provençal rosé is dry and refreshing, built for the apéritif hour and Mediterranean food. The main appellation is Côtes de Provence, with Coteaux dAix-en-Provence and others alongside.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a dry, elegant, pale rosé; a summer or apéritif wine; or a match for salads, seafood, and Mediterranean food.

Bandol — Provences serious reds

Bandol is Provence's most prestigious appellation, a coastal zone where Mourvèdre ripens fully to make deep, structured, ageworthy reds — dark fruit, leather, wild herbs, firm tannin — that can improve for a decade or more. Bandol also makes a highly regarded, more structured rosé.
Serve at: 16–18°C reds.
Recommend when: the user wants a serious, structured Mediterranean red (Mourvèdre), a match for game or lamb, or a rosé with more substance.

Cassis & other Provence whites

Beyond rosé and Bandol, Provence makes distinctive whites — notably Cassis (a small coastal appellation, unrelated to the blackcurrant liqueur), producing fresh, textured whites from Marsanne, Clairette, and others, classic with bouillabaisse and Mediterranean seafood.
Recommend when: the user wants a Provençal white for seafood, or something beyond rosé from the region.

Southwest France — overview

Southwest France ("Sud-Ouest") is a diverse patchwork of appellations inland and south of Bordeaux, sharing some Bordeaux grapes but rich in distinctive local varieties. It is one of France's best sources of characterful, great-value, individual wines, both red and white, dry and sweet.
Recommend when: the user wants distinctive, affordable, off-the-beaten-path French wines with local character.

Southwest reds — Cahors, Madiran & more

- Cahors — dark, structured red from Malbec (locally Côt/Auxerrois); the historic home of the grape, more rustic and savory than Argentine Malbec.
- Madiran — powerful, tannic red from the local Tannat grape; deeply colored, ageworthy, needs time or food (classic with cassoulet and duck).
- Bergerac / Pécharmant — Bordeaux-style Merlot/Cabernet blends near Bordeaux, at friendlier prices.
- Fronton (Négrette), Marcillac (Fer Servadou/Mansois), Gaillac (many local grapes) — distinctive regional reds.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a dark, structured red (Cahors Malbec, Madiran Tannat), a Bordeaux alternative (Bergerac), or something unusual and local.

Southwest whites & sweet wines

- Jurançon (near the Pyrenees) — from Petit and Gros Manseng; both a racy dry white (sec) and a honeyed, high-acid sweet white (moelleux), the latter a classic with foie gras.
- Gaillac — dry, sweet, and sparkling whites from local grapes (Mauzac, Loin de lŒil).
- Monbazillac — botrytized sweet white near Bergerac (Sémillon-based), a great-value Sauternes alternative.
- Côtes de Gascogne (IGP) — crisp, zesty, inexpensive dry whites (often Colombard/Ugni Blanc), hugely popular as everyday value.
Recommend when: the user wants a racy or sweet Manseng (Jurançon), a value dessert wine (Monbazillac), or a cheap, crisp everyday white (Côtes de Gascogne).

Quick regional summary beaujolais

- Beaujolais: granite hills south of Burgundy; Gamay — light, juicy, chillable reds; ten serious crus (Morgon, Moulin-à-Vent, Fleurie) over-deliver on value; Nouveau is the November party wine.
- Provence: Mediterranean southeast; benchmark dry rosé (Grenache/Cinsault/Syrah/Mourvèdre); serious Mourvèdre reds in Bandol; whites in Cassis.
- Southwest France: diverse local grapes — Malbec (Cahors), Tannat (Madiran), Manseng (Jurançon), botrytized Monbazillac, value whites (Côtes de Gascogne); characterful and affordable.

Bordeaux — overview

Bordeaux is the world's most famous fine-wine region, a large area in southwest France centered on the city of Bordeaux and shaped by the Gironde estuary and its two rivers, the Garonne and the Dordogne. It is a maritime climate — moderated by the Atlantic — which brings both the risk of unsettled weather at flowering and harvest and the gentle conditions that let its grapes develop slowly. Bordeaux makes dry reds (the great majority), dry whites, and some of the world's greatest sweet whites. Its wines are almost always blends, and its defining geographic split is Left Bank vs Right Bank.
Recommend when: the user wants a classic, ageworthy blended red, a benchmark to understand Cabernet or Merlot, or a great sweet wine (Sauternes).

The Bordeaux blend — red

Red Bordeaux is built from a core of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, supported by Cabernet Franc and smaller amounts of Petit Verdot, Malbec, and Carménère. Blending is the point: it balances Cabernet's structure and ageability against Merlot's flesh and approachability, and provides insurance against vintage variation (the varieties ripen at different times). The proportions depend on which bank — and which soils — the wine comes from.
Recommend when: the user wants a structured, savory, food-friendly red with the capacity to age.

Left Bank — Cabernet Sauvignon country

The Left Bank (west of the Gironde/Garonne) has gravelly soils that suit Cabernet Sauvignon, which dominates its blends. The wines are firm, structured, tannic when young, with blackcurrant, cedar, and graphite notes, and they age for decades. Its key zones:
- Médoc and Haut-Médoc — the broad northern peninsula.
- Communal appellations of the Haut-Médoc: Saint-Estèphe (firm, structured), Pauillac (the most powerful and prestigious; home to several First Growths), Saint-Julien (balanced, classic), Margaux (perfumed, elegant).
- Pessac-Léognan / Graves — south of the city; gravelly reds plus fine dry whites.
Serve at: 16–18°C, decant young wines.
Recommend when: the user wants the most structured, ageworthy, Cabernet-driven style of Bordeaux.

Right Bank — Merlot country

The Right Bank (east/north, around the Dordogne) has clay and limestone soils that favor Merlot and Cabernet Franc. The wines are plumper, softer, and approachable earlier than the Left Bank, though the best age superbly. Its key appellations:
- Pomerol — small, clay-rich; produces the most opulent, velvety Merlot-based wines (Pétrus is its icon). No official classification.
- Saint-Émilion — larger, historic, limestone-influenced; Merlot and Cabernet Franc; has its own classification led by Premiers Grands Crus Classés.
- Satellite and outlying appellations (Lalande-de-Pomerol, the Saint-Émilion satellites, Fronsac, Castillon, Bourg, Blaye) offer better value in a similar style.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a softer, rounder, plummier Bordeaux, approachable younger, or a Merlot-led red.

Bordeaux classifications

- The 1855 Classification — ranked the top Médoc (plus Château Haut-Brion in Graves) reds into five tiers of Cru Classé, from First to Fifth Growth, based on price/reputation at the time. Still influential; largely unchanged. The First Growths are Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion, and (promoted in 1973) Mouton Rothschild.
- 1855 also classified Sauternes/Barsac sweet wines, with Château dYquem alone at the top (Premier Cru Supérieur).
- Saint-Émilion has its own classification, revised periodically (Premier Grand Cru Classé A and B, Grand Cru Classé).
- Pomerol has no classification at all — reputation is set by the market.
- Cru Bourgeois — a separate tier for quality Médoc estates below the classified growths; good value.
Practical use: classification signals prestige and price tier, but the sommelier should stress that Cru Bourgeois and satellite appellations often over-deliver on value.

Dry white Bordeaux

Dry white Bordeaux blends Sauvignon Blanc (zip, citrus, grassy aromatics) with Sémillon (body, waxy texture, ageability), sometimes with a little Muscadelle. Styles range from crisp, unoaked, everyday whites (much labeled simply Bordeaux Blanc or Entre-Deux-Mers) to serious barrel-fermented whites from Pessac-Léognan that rival white Burgundy and age for years.
Serve at: 8–11°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a citrusy dry white for seafood (everyday style) or a textured, ageworthy white for richer dishes (Pessac-Léognan).

Sweet white Bordeaux — Sauternes & Barsac

Sauternes and its neighbor Barsac make some of the world's greatest sweet wines from Sémillon (mainly), Sauvignon Blanc, and Muscadelle affected by noble rot (Botrytis cinerea). The botrytis fungus shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugars and flavors, giving lusciously sweet, honeyed, apricot-and-marmalade wines balanced by high acidity, capable of ageing for decades. Château dYquem is the benchmark. Neighboring appellations (Cadillac, Loupiac, Sainte-Croix-du-Mont) offer similar styles for less.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Classic pairing: foie gras, blue cheese (Roquefort), fruit tarts.
Recommend when: the user wants a great dessert wine, or asks about foie gras or blue cheese pairings.

Entre-Deux-Mers and everyday Bordeaux

Entre-Deux-Mers (between the two rivers) is a large zone known mainly for crisp dry white. Much of Bordeaux's volume, though, is everyday red labeled Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur — Merlot-dominant, soft, and for early drinking. Quality is variable, but good producers make honest, affordable claret.
Recommend when: the user wants an affordable, easy-drinking weeknight red or a crisp inexpensive white.

Bordeaux vintage sensitivity

Because of its maritime climate, Bordeaux is genuinely vintage-sensitive — weather at flowering and harvest makes or breaks a year, more so than in reliably warm regions. Great recent red vintages are talked about specifically (e.g. 2005, 2009, 2010, 2015, 2016). This matters for cellaring and buying: a modest vintage is for earlier drinking, a great one rewards patience.
Practical use: when a user is buying to age or spending seriously, vintage guidance matters more in Bordeaux than in most regions.

Quick regional summary bordeaux

- Left Bank: gravel, Cabernet Sauvignon-led, firm and ageworthy; Médoc communes (Pauillac, Margaux, Saint-Julien, Saint-Estèphe) + Pessac-Léognan.
- Right Bank: clay/limestone, Merlot-led, plusher; Pomerol and Saint-Émilion.
- Whites: dry Sauvignon/Sémillon blends (crisp to serious); great sweet wines in Sauternes/Barsac.
- Classifications: 1855 (Médoc + Sauternes), Saint-Émilions own, Cru Bourgeois for value; Pomerol unclassified.
- Character throughout: blends, maritime climate, vintage sensitivity, ageworthiness.

Burgundy — overview

Burgundy (Bourgogne) is a long, narrow region in eastern France that represents the world's most detailed expression of terroir — the idea that a specific plot of land gives a wine a specific character. Almost all Burgundy is single-variety: Pinot Noir for reds, Chardonnay for whites. What varies is the place, sliced into a fine hierarchy of vineyards. Holdings are small and fragmented (a legacy of inheritance law), so the producer (domaine) matters as much as the vineyard. Burgundy runs north to south: Chablis, the Côte dOr (Côte de Nuits + Côte de Beaune), the Côte Chalonnaise, and the Mâconnais.
Recommend when: the user wants the benchmark for Pinot Noir or Chardonnay, is interested in terroir, or wants an elegant, food-versatile wine.

The Burgundy quality hierarchy

Burgundy classifies vineyards, not producers, in four ascending tiers:
- Regional (Bourgogne) — the broadest appellation; grapes from anywhere in the region. Everyday Burgundy.
- Village — wines from a named commune (e.g. Gevrey-Chambertin, Meursault), blended from vineyards around that village.
- Premier Cru (1er Cru) — specific superior named vineyards within a village (labeled village + vineyard name).
- Grand Cru — the pinnacle: a small number of historic vineyards so renowned they stand alone on the label (e.g. Chambertin, Montrachet, Corton).
Practical use: the hierarchy is the single best guide to price and ambition in Burgundy — but producer quality can make a village wine outshine a lesser grower's Premier Cru.

Chablis — steely northern Chardonnay

Chablis, in Burgundy's cool far north, makes Chardonnay in a distinctively lean, high-acid, mineral style — green apple, citrus, oyster-shell, "flinty" — often unoaked or only lightly oaked. Its Kimmeridgian limestone soils (full of tiny marine fossils) are credited with its signature stony character. It has its own hierarchy: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru, and seven Grand Cru vineyards. Spring frost is its perennial hazard.
Serve at: 8–11°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a crisp, mineral, unoaked-style Chardonnay; a match for oysters, shellfish, or sushi; or a leaner alternative to rich Chardonnay.

Côte de Nuits — the great reds

The Côte de Nuits, the northern half of the Côte dOr, is Pinot Noir's greatest home — a narrow strip of slopes producing the most powerful, structured, long-lived red Burgundies. Its villages read like a roll call of legendary names: Gevrey-Chambertin, Morey-Saint-Denis, Chambolle-Musigny, Vougeot, Vosne-Romanée (home to Romanée-Conti and other Grands Crus), and Nuits-Saint-Georges. Most of Burgundy's red Grands Crus are here.
Serve at: 14–16°C.
Recommend when: the user wants the finest, most ageworthy Pinot Noir, or a special-occasion red for duck, game, or mushroom dishes.
