data.content:
Roussillon dry whites & Côtes Catalanes

Beyond the fortified tradition, Roussillon makes haunting dry whites from an exotic palette of grapes — often old-vine Grenache Blanc and Gris, Macabeu, Carignan Blanc, and others — many sold under the IGP Côtes Catalanes designation. A wave of independent, often natural-leaning producers has proven that Roussillon can make great, ageworthy dry wine whose character comes from its schist and granite soils rather than international fashion. These whites are textured, mineral, and distinctive.
Recommend when: the user wants an original, mineral, characterful dry white off the beaten path, or is exploring natural/independent southern French wine.

Quick regional summary languedoc

- Languedoc: vast, warm, coastal; GSM + Carignan/Cinsault reds (80% of output), Mediterranean white blends, crisp Picpoul de Pinet, schist-driven Faugères, sweet Muscat VDN. Transformed from bulk to value-and-character.
- Roussillon: hotter, Catalan, mountainous; old-vine Grenache; famous for fortified Banyuls/Maury/Rivesaltes VDN, powerful dry Collioure reds, and exotic mineral dry whites (Côtes Catalanes).
- Shared thread: garrigue-herb character, old bushvines, a strong independent/organic/natural producer culture, and excellent value relative to more famous French regions.

Loire Valley — overview

The Loire is France's longest river, and its wine region stretches across the north-center of the country from the Atlantic coast inland toward Sancerre. It is a cool-climate region famous above all for white wine and for extraordinary versatility — dry, off-dry, sweet, sparkling, plus crisp reds and rosés. Four broad zones run west to east: the Pays Nantais (Muscadet), Anjou-Saumur, Touraine, and the Central Vineyards (Sancerre/Pouilly-Fumé). The Loire is a haven of high-acid, food-friendly, often great-value wines and a hub of natural-wine production.
Recommend when: the user wants crisp, mineral whites; food-friendly high-acid wines; or distinctive, characterful, often-affordable bottles.

Muscadet (Pays Nantais)

At the Atlantic mouth of the Loire, Muscadet is made from the Melon de Bourgogne grape — light, dry, crisp, and saline, with green-apple and citrus notes. The best is labeled sur lie (aged on its lees), which adds a subtle creaminess and depth. It is the classic oyster and shellfish wine, and serious cru-village Muscadet can age and gain surprising complexity.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user is eating oysters, shellfish, or seafood, or wants a bone-dry, saline, affordable white.

Sauvignon Blanc — Sancerre & Pouilly-Fumé

At the eastern end (the Central Vineyards), Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are the benchmark for Sauvignon Blanc: crisp, aromatic, and mineral, with notes of citrus, gooseberry, green herbs, and a flinty/smoky edge (the "fumé" in Pouilly-Fumé refers to the flinty soils). These are more restrained and mineral than New Zealand Sauvignon — the classic elegant expression. Sancerre also makes a little Pinot Noir red and rosé.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a refined, mineral Sauvignon Blanc; a match for goat cheese (the classic Sancerre pairing), oysters, or salads.

Chenin Blanc — the Loires great white

Chenin Blanc is the Loire's most versatile and ageworthy white grape, centered in Anjou, Saumur, and Touraine. Its high acidity lets it make wines at every sweetness level:
- Vouvray and Montlouis (Touraine) — dry (sec), off-dry (demi-sec), sweet (moelleux), and sparkling, all from Chenin.
- Savennières (Anjou) — bone-dry, powerful, mineral, ageworthy Chenin.
- Coteaux du Layon, Quarts de Chaume, Bonnezeaux (Anjou) — botrytized sweet Chenin, honeyed and long-lived.
Chenin shows honey, quince, apple, and damp-straw notes, with piercing acidity that keeps even sweet versions fresh.
Serve at: 8–11°C dry; 8–10°C sweet.
Recommend when: the user wants a textured, high-acid white (Savennières/dry Vouvray), a versatile food white, a sparkling alternative, or an ageworthy sweet wine.
data.section_title: Chenin Blanc — the Loires great white

data.content:
Loire reds — Cabernet Franc

The Loire's serious reds are Cabernet Franc, centered in Touraine and Anjou-Saumur: Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil, and Saumur-Champigny. These are aromatic, medium-bodied, refreshing reds with red-fruit, graphite, and leafy-herbal notes and often a fine, silky texture. Cooler than Bordeaux's Cabernet Franc, they're food-friendly and can be lightly chilled.
Serve at: 14–16°C, lightly chilled in summer.
Recommend when: the user wants a lighter, aromatic, food-friendly red; a summer red; or a match for charcuterie and roast poultry.

Loire rosé & sparkling

- Rosé d'Anjou — off-dry, fruity pink; Cabernet d'Anjou — sweeter rosé; both easy-drinking.
- Rosé de Loire — dry rosé.
- Crémant de Loire — traditional-method sparkling, often Chenin-led; excellent value bubbly.
- Sparkling Vouvray/Saumur — Chenin-based fizz with real character.
Recommend when: the user wants an affordable, characterful sparkling (Crémant de Loire) or an easy fruity rosé.

The Loire & natural wine

The Loire, especially Touraine and Anjou, is one of France's great hubs of organic, biodynamic, and natural winemaking. Its high-acid grapes (Chenin, Cabernet Franc, Melon, Sauvignon) suit low-intervention styles, and many cult natural producers work here. Expect to encounter Loire wines in natural-wine bars and lists.
Recommend when: the user is exploring natural wine or wants low-intervention, characterful bottles.

Quick regional summary loire

- Pays Nantais: Muscadet (Melon de Bourgogne) — dry, saline, oyster wine, best sur lie.
- Central Vineyards: Sancerre & Pouilly-Fumé — benchmark mineral Sauvignon Blanc.
- Anjou-Saumur-Touraine: Chenin Blanc in every style (dry Savennières, versatile Vouvray, sweet Layon, sparkling); Cabernet Franc reds (Chinon, Bourgueil, Saumur-Champigny).
- Throughout: high acidity, food-friendliness, great value, and a strong natural-wine culture.

New Zealand — overview

New Zealand is a cool, maritime, southerly wine country that rose to global fame astonishingly fast, largely on the back of one wine: Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc. Its clean, intense, aromatic style — driven by cool temperatures, bright sunlight, and a long growing season — defines modern New Zealand wine, but the country also makes world-class Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and aromatic whites. Labeled by grape variety; quality-focused and largely screwcapped (NZ led the shift away from cork).
Recommend when: the user wants intensely aromatic, zesty whites, or cool-climate Pinot Noir.

Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc

Marlborough, at the top of the South Island, is New Zealand's largest and most famous region, and its Sauvignon Blanc is a global phenomenon: piercingly aromatic, zesty, and pungent, with passionfruit, gooseberry, grapefruit, green capsicum, and a razor-sharp acidity. It's the benchmark for the punchy, fruit-explosive style of the grape (a contrast to the more restrained, mineral Loire version). Marlborough also makes excellent Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, aromatic whites, and traditional-method sparkling.
Serve at: 7–9°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a bold, aromatic, zesty white; a crowd-pleasing Sauvignon Blanc; or a match for goat cheese, salads, seafood, or Asian food.

New Zealand Pinot Noir

Pinot Noir is New Zealand's flagship red, made in an elegant, perfumed, cool-climate style across several regions:
- Central Otago — the world's southernmost wine region; dramatic, continental (not maritime); ripe, vibrant, structured Pinot with intense red and dark fruit. NZ's most famous Pinot.
- Martinborough / Wairarapa — small, top-quality, savory and structured Pinot.
- Marlborough — lighter, fruit-forward, good value Pinot.
- Nelson, Waipara/North Canterbury — additional cool Pinot sources.
Serve at: 14–16°C.
Recommend when: the user wants an aromatic, elegant, fruit-driven cool-climate Pinot Noir; Central Otago for ripe intensity, Martinborough for savory structure.

Other New Zealand wines

- Chardonnay — increasingly excellent, from restrained to Burgundian (strong in Hawke's Bay, Gisborne, Marlborough).
- Aromatic whites — Riesling (dry to off-dry), Pinot Gris, and Gewürztraminer thrive in the cool climate.
- Hawke's Bay (North Island) — warmer; New Zealand's best region for Bordeaux-style reds (Merlot/Cabernet) and Syrah (elegant, peppery), plus Chardonnay. The Gimblett Gravels sub-zone is prized for reds.
- Sparkling — high-quality traditional-method fizz (Marlborough).
Recommend when: the user wants NZ Chardonnay, aromatic whites, or a cool-climate Bordeaux blend/Syrah (Hawke's Bay).

Quick regional summary new-zealand

- New Zealand: cool, maritime, southerly; screwcap country; labeled by grape.
- Marlborough: the famous zesty, aromatic Sauvignon Blanc (passionfruit/gooseberry); also Pinot and sparkling.
- Pinot Noir: elegant and perfumed — Central Otago (ripe, intense), Martinborough (savory), Marlborough (value).
- Hawke's Bay (North Island): warmer; Bordeaux blends & Syrah (Gimblett Gravels), Chardonnay.
- Also: fine Chardonnay and aromatic Riesling/Pinot Gris/Gewürztraminer.

Port — overview

Port (Porto) is a fortified sweet wine from the terraced schist slopes of the Douro Valley in northern Portugal, traditionally aged and shipped from Vila Nova de Gaia near the city of Porto. It's made by adding grape spirit partway through fermentation, which stops the yeast and leaves natural grape sweetness while raising alcohol to ~19–20%. Made from indigenous Douro grapes — Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão — Port spans fresh fruity styles to profound, decades-aged wines. The two great families are Ruby (fruit-driven, aged in bottle) and Tawny (oxidative, aged in barrel).
Recommend when: the user wants a sweet fortified red; a dessert or cheese wine; a wine to cellar; or a classic after-dinner drink.

Ruby-style Ports (fruit-driven, bottle-aged)

These emphasize fresh, dark fruit and are aged mostly in bottle:
- Ruby — young, simple, fruity, inexpensive; drink now.
- Reserve Ruby — a step up in quality and concentration.
- Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) — from a single year, aged 4–6 years before bottling; rich, approachable, great value, usually ready to drink.
- Vintage Port — the pinnacle: only declared in the best years (~3 times a decade), from the finest wine, bottled young after ~2 years and then aged in bottle for decades. Powerful, tannic, and profound; needs long cellaring and throws a heavy sediment (decant it). The longest-lived style.
- Single Quinta Vintage — vintage-style from a single estate, often in undeclared years; excellent value for the quality.
- Crusted — a blend of vintages, bottled unfiltered, forming a "crust"; a value stand-in for vintage.
Serve at: 16–18°C; decant vintage and crusted.
Recommend when: the user wants rich dark fruit (LBV for value-now, Vintage for cellaring); a match for chocolate, blue cheese, or the classic Stilton pairing.

Tawny-style Ports (oxidative, barrel-aged)

These age in cask, gaining a nutty, oxidative, amber character and losing color:
- Tawny (basic) — often just a lighter blend; simple.
- Aged Tawny — 10, 20, 30, 40 Year — the connoisseur's Port; barrel-aged to the stated average age, giving nutty, caramel, dried-fig, and spice notes with a smooth, mellow texture. Ready to drink, no decanting needed. 20 Year is often cited as the sweet spot.
- Colheita — a single-vintage tawny, barrel-aged for many years (unlike Vintage Port, which is bottle-aged); labeled with its harvest year. Nutty, complex, and often remarkable value for its age.
Serve at: 12–16°C (can be lightly chilled).
Recommend when: the user wants a nutty, smooth, mellow style; an easy after-dinner wine needing no decanting; a match for caramel/nut desserts, tarts, or hard cheese.

White & Rosé Port

- White Port — from white Douro grapes; ranges dry to sweet. Served chilled, often in the popular "Port tónico" (white Port and tonic with mint and lemon) — a refreshing apéritif.
- Rosé Port — a modern, pink, fruity, chilled style for cocktails.
Serve at: 6–8°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a fortified apéritif, a Port cocktail base, or a summer/aperitivo option.

Serving & keeping Port

- Vintage & Crusted — decant off their heavy sediment; drink within a day or two of opening.
- LBV — usually filtered; ready to drink, keeps a week or two open.
- Tawny (aged & Colheita) — ready to drink, no decanting; keeps for weeks (oxidative styles are robust).
- White/Rosé — serve cold, drink fresh.
Classic pairings: Vintage/LBV with blue cheese (Stilton) and dark chocolate; aged Tawny with nutty/caramel desserts and hard cheese.
Recommend when: the user asks how to serve, decant, or keep a Port.

Madeira — overview

Madeira is a fortified wine from the volcanic Portuguese island of Madeira in the Atlantic, and one of the most extraordinary and long-lived wines in the world. Its defining process is deliberate heating and oxidation — historically wines were seasoned on long sea voyages through the tropics; today they're heated in warm rooms (canteiro, gentle natural warming for the best; estufagem, faster tank heating for everyday). This "cooked" ageing gives Madeira its trademark searing acidity, caramelized richness, and near-indestructibility: an opened bottle stays fresh for months or years, and old Madeira can live a century-plus.
Recommend when: the user wants an intensely long-lived wine, a tangy fortified style, a cooking wine, or a piece of wine history.

Madeira — the styles (driest to sweetest)

Madeira's classic styles are named for their grapes, running dry to sweet:
- Sercial — the driest; light, high-acid, almond and citrus, bracing. A substantial apéritif (more than a Fino sherry).
- Verdelho — off-dry; smoky, honeyed, medium; before or after meals.
- Bual (Boal) — medium-sweet; richer, raisiny, with a smoky edge; a dessert style.
- Malmsey (Malvasia) — the sweetest; dark, fragrant, soft, and rich, yet cut by Madeira's signature sharp tang.
- Tinta Negra — the most-planted grape, behind much everyday Madeira across all sweetness levels; also modern varietal bottlings.
Labels may show a style/grape, a sweetness term (Dry, Medium Dry, Medium Rich, Rich), or an age (5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50+ years); single-vintage Colheita and ancient Frasqueira/Vintage Madeiras exist too.
Serve at: 12–16°C (Sercial/Verdelho cooler; Bual/Malmsey slightly warmer).
Recommend when: matching sweetness — Sercial as a tangy apéritif, Verdelho as a versatile sipper, Bual/Malmsey for dessert (cakes, nuts, dried fruit, chocolate).

Why Madeira lasts

Because Madeira has already been oxidized and heated in its making, it is essentially impervious to the things that ruin other wines. Once opened, it doesn't spoil the way table wine does — making it uniquely practical as well as historic (and an excellent, genuinely flavorful cooking wine). It has the strongest claim to being the world's longest-living wine.
Recommend when: the user worries about an open bottle going off, wants a wine to keep indefinitely, or asks for a good fortified cooking wine.

Quick summary port-madeira

- Port (Douro, sweet fortified red, ~20% abv):
  - Ruby family (fruit, bottle-aged): Ruby → LBV (value) → Vintage (cellar for decades, decant) → Single Quinta → Crusted.
  - Tawny family (nutty, barrel-aged): Tawny → 10/20/30/40 Year (smooth, no decant) → Colheita (single-vintage tawny).
  - White/Rosé Port: chilled apéritifs and cocktails (Port tónico).
- Madeira (volcanic island, heated & oxidized, near-immortal): Sercial (dry) → Verdelho → Bual → Malmsey (sweetest); Tinta Negra for everyday; age-dated and Frasqueira for the finest.

Portugal — overview

Portugal punches far above its size in wine, thanks to an unmatched treasury of indigenous grape varieties — hundreds of them, largely unique to the country — and a wide range of climates from the cool, wet Atlantic northwest to the hot, dry interior. Long known abroad mainly for fortified Port and Madeira, Portugal is now celebrated for distinctive, great-value dry table wines with a characteristic freshness and "bite." Its classification runs from Vinho (basic) through Vinho Regional (IGP) to DOC (top tier).
Recommend when: the user wants distinctive, indigenous-grape wines; great value; or something off the beaten path.

Vinho Verde

Vinho Verde ("green wine," meaning young, not green in color) comes from the cool, rainy, green northwest. Classically it's a light, low-alcohol, high-acid, slightly spritzy white — crisp and refreshing, made from grapes like Alvarinho (the same as Spanish Albariño, best in the Monção e Melgaço subregion), Loureiro, Arinto, and Trajadura. Modern serious Vinho Verde, especially varietal Alvarinho, can be fuller and age-worthy. The classic cheap-and-cheerful patio white, but with a quality tier above.
Serve at: 7–9°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a light, crisp, low-alcohol, refreshing white; a summer or seafood wine; or serious Alvarinho.

Douro (table wines)

The dramatic, terraced Douro Valley — the same schist slopes that make Port — also produces some of Portugal's finest dry red table wines, from the same grapes as Port: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinto Cão, and others. These are deep, structured, aromatic reds — dark fruit, floral notes, minerality from schist — ranging from powerful and ageworthy to more elegant modern styles. Increasingly fine dry whites too (from Rabigato, Viosinho, Gouveio). A benchmark for Portuguese red.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a structured, aromatic, ageworthy dry red; a match for red meat and game; or top Portuguese wine.

Dão

Dão, in granite hills further south, was once known for tough, tannic co-op reds but is now a source of elegant, aromatic, terroir-driven wines. Reds are led by Touriga Nacional and Jaen (Mencía) with others — perfumed, fresh, medium-bodied, with fine tannins and good ageing potential. Whites from Encruzado are among Portugal's finest — textured, mineral, ageworthy. Often likened to a Portuguese Burgundy for its elegance.
Serve at: 16–18°C reds; 10–12°C whites.
Recommend when: the user wants an elegant, aromatic, fresh Portuguese red, or a serious white (Encruzado).

Bairrada

Bairrada, near the Atlantic between Dão and the coast, is defined by the Baga grape — high in acid and tannin, late-ripening, and (unusually for Portugal) usually unblended. Traditional Baga is dark, structured, and long-lived (sometimes compared to Nebbiolo); modern producers use gentler techniques for prettier, more Burgundian styles. Bairrada also makes fresh whites (Bical, Maria Gomes/Fernão Pires) and has a strong traditional-method sparkling tradition (white and rosé) thanks to its Atlantic freshness and clay-limestone soils.
Serve at: 16–18°C reds.
Recommend when: the user wants a structured, ageworthy, high-acid red (Baga), a Portuguese sparkling, or a fresh Atlantic white.

Lisboa & Península de Setúbal

- Lisboa (formerly Estremadura), the coastal strip north of Lisbon, is a large region of everyday value wines and some rising stars, including historic small DOCs like Colares (ungrafted vines in coastal sand) and Bucelas (Arinto whites).
- Península de Setúbal, south of Lisbon, is famous for Moscatel de Setúbal — a rich, aromatic fortified Muscat dessert wine — plus good reds from Castelão and others.
Recommend when: the user wants value coastal wines, a rare sandy-soil curiosity (Colares), or an aromatic fortified Muscat (Setúbal).

Alentejo

The hot, sunny, rolling Alentejo in the south is Portugal's answer to a warm New World region — making ripe, smooth, fruit-forward, approachable reds (from Aragonez/Tempranillo, Trincadeira, Alicante Bouschet, and others) and increasingly good whites (Antão Vaz, Arinto). Reliable crowd-pleasers and strong value; also a home of clay-amphora (talha) winemaking, a Roman-era tradition still practiced.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a ripe, smooth, easy-drinking red; a crowd-pleaser; or a warm-climate value wine.

Other regions & Portuguese whites

- Beira Interior, Távora-Varosa, Trás-os-Montes — inland northern regions with cool-climate and high-altitude potential.
- Portuguese white grapes worth knowing: Alvarinho (aromatic, citrus), Arinto (racy acidity, ageworthy), Encruzado (textured, mineral), Antão Vaz (full, southern), Fernão Pires/Maria Gomes (aromatic).
- Rosé: Portugal's historic sweetish rosé (the Mateus/Lancers style) has a modern dry counterpart.
Recommend when: the user wants a specific Portuguese white style, or is exploring lesser-known regions.

Quick regional summary portugal

- Vinho Verde (northwest): light, crisp, spritzy whites; Alvarinho at the top.
- Douro: structured, aromatic dry reds (Touriga Nacional & co.) from Port country; fine whites too.
- Dão: elegant, aromatic reds (Touriga Nacional/Jaen); superb Encruzado whites.
- Bairrada: structured Baga reds; sparkling; fresh whites.
- Lisboa/Setúbal: value coastal wines; Colares curiosity; Moscatel de Setúbal (fortified Muscat).
- Alentejo: ripe, smooth, fruit-forward reds; value crowd-pleasers; talha (amphora) tradition.
- Signature: hundreds of indigenous grapes, Atlantic freshness, and outstanding value.

Rhône Valley — overview

The Rhône Valley follows the Rhône river through southeastern France, from Vienne (below Lyon) south toward Avignon. It splits into two very different halves: the Northern Rhône, a narrow, cooler, steep-sloped zone devoted to Syrah and a handful of whites; and the Southern Rhône, a warm, broad, Mediterranean landscape of Grenache-based blends. Together they make some of France's greatest and best-value reds.
Recommend when: the user wants savory, structured reds (north) or warm, generous Mediterranean blends (south).

Northern Rhône — Syrah country

The Northern Rhône is Syrah's spiritual home. On steep granite slopes along the river, Syrah makes dark, structured, savory reds marked by black pepper, smoked meat, olive, and violet. Reds here are 100% Syrah (though small amounts of white grapes may be co-fermented for perfume). The zone is small but prestigious, its top appellations among the most collectible wines in France.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a savory, peppery, ageworthy Syrah — the benchmark for the grape.

Northern Rhône appellations

- Côte-Rôtie — the "roasted slope"; perfumed, elegant Syrah, traditionally co-fermented with a splash of white Viognier for aromatic lift. Steep, terraced.
- Hermitage — the grandest; powerful, dense, long-lived Syrah from a single famous hill. Also fine whites.
- Crozes-Hermitage — the large surrounding appellation; approachable, good-value Syrah.
- Cornas — 100% Syrah, dark and rustic-powerful, no white permitted.
- Saint-Joseph — versatile Syrah, lighter and more approachable; some white.
- Condrieu — white only, 100% Viognier; lush, aromatic apricot-and-honeysuckle wine, best drunk young.
Recommend when: matching taste — Côte-Rôtie for perfume, Hermitage for power, Crozes/Saint-Joseph for value, Condrieu for aromatic whites.

Northern Rhône whites — Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne

Beyond red Syrah, the Northern Rhône makes distinctive whites:
- Viognier — the star of Condrieu; full-bodied, perfumed, apricot and blossom, low acidity.
- Marsanne and Roussanne — the pair behind white Hermitage, Crozes, and Saint-Joseph; full, nutty, honeyed, textured whites that can age surprisingly well.
Recommend when: the user wants a rich, aromatic white (Viognier) or a full, ageworthy white blend (Marsanne/Roussanne).

data.content:
Southern Rhône — Grenache-based blends

The Southern Rhône is warm, sunny, and Mediterranean, and its reds are blends built on Grenache, supported by Syrah and Mourvèdre (the "GSM" trio), with Cinsault and others. The wines are generous, warm, and fruit-forward — red berries, garrigue herbs, pepper, and spice — with soft-to-firm tannins depending on the blend. This is the volume heart of the Rhône and a reliable source of value.
Serve at: 15–17°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a warm, generous, herb-scented red for grilled meats, stews, or Mediterranean food.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape

The most famous Southern Rhône appellation, Châteauneuf-du-Pape permits up to 13 grape varieties (18 counting color variants) but is Grenache-led, blended with Syrah, Mourvèdre, and others. Famous for its large, heat-retaining rounded stones (galets roulés) in some vineyards, it makes rich, warming, spicy reds of 14–15%+ alcohol, capable of ageing. A small amount of full-bodied white Châteauneuf is also made.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a rich, powerful, warming Southern Rhône red for hearty dishes, or a benchmark GSM blend.

Southern Rhône villages & value tiers

The Southern Rhône has a useful quality ladder:
- Côtes du Rhône — the broad regional appellation; everyday, fruit-forward, excellent value reds.
- Côtes du Rhône-Villages — a step up, from better villages, some allowed to append their name.
- Named cru villages — the top tier alongside Châteauneuf: Gigondas (structured, Grenache-led, a value alternative to Châteauneuf), Vacqueyras (warm, spicy), Rasteau (rich; also fortified sweet Grenache), Cairanne, Lirac, and others.
- Tavel — a cru dedicated entirely to dry rosé; deep-colored, full-bodied, serious pink wine.
Recommend when: matching budget and style — Côtes du Rhône for value, Villages/crus for a step up, Gigondas/Vacqueyras as Châteauneuf alternatives, Tavel for serious rosé.

Southern Rhône sweet & fortified

The Southern Rhône makes Vins Doux Naturels (fortified sweet wines): Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise (aromatic, grapey sweet Muscat) and Rasteau (sweet fortified Grenache, red or amber). These are dessert and apéritif specialties.
Recommend when: the user wants an aromatic sweet apéritif (Beaumes-de-Venise Muscat) or a port-like fortified red (Rasteau).

Rhône & climate

The Northern Rhône's steep slopes and cooler climate preserve Syrah's pepper and freshness, while the warm Southern Rhône ripens Grenache to high sugar and alcohol. Harvest dates across the valley have moved earlier with climate change, and growers increasingly seek freshness — planting on cooler aspects and picking earlier — to keep alcohol in check.
Recommend when: the user asks why northern and southern Rhône taste so different, or about alcohol levels.

Quick regional summary rhone

- Northern Rhône: cool, steep, granite; 100% Syrah reds (Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage, Crozes, Cornas, Saint-Joseph) — savory, peppery, ageworthy; whites from Viognier (Condrieu), Marsanne, Roussanne.
- Southern Rhône: warm, Mediterranean; Grenache-Syrah-Mourvèdre blends (Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Gigondas, Côtes du Rhône) — generous, spicy, herbal; serious rosé (Tavel); fortified Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise.
- Value sweet spot: Côtes du Rhône(-Villages) reds and northern Crozes/Saint-Joseph.

South Africa — overview

South Africa bridges Old and New World in style: long-established (winemaking dates to the 1650s) yet re-energized since the end of apartheid and its return to world markets in the 1990s. Vineyards cluster in the Western Cape, in a Mediterranean climate cooled by the Atlantic and the Cape Doctor (a strong southeasterly wind). The scene today is dynamic, with a celebrated new generation making fresh, characterful, terroir-driven wines — often from old bushvines — alongside great value at every level. Labeled by grape, with WO (Wine of Origin) denoting geographic origin.
Recommend when: the user wants distinctive, food-friendly, Old-meets-New-World wines, often at excellent value; or old-vine and artisan bottlings.

Chenin Blanc — the signature white

Chenin Blanc (historically "Steen") is South Africa's most-planted grape and its calling card — the country has the world's largest Chenin plantings, including precious old bushvines. Styles run from fresh, easy, and fruity to serious, textured, barrel-aged, age-worthy whites of real complexity (honey, quince, stone fruit, a mineral core). Old-vine Cape Chenin is one of the wine world's great values and a source of genuinely world-class whites.
Serve at: 9–11°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a textured, food-friendly white; a great-value serious white; or an alternative to Chardonnay/white Burgundy.

Pinotage — the local red

Pinotage is South Africa's own grape, a crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault created in 1925. It makes deeply colored, robust reds with dark fruit, smoke, and (in riper styles) a distinctive banana/rooibos or mocha note. Divisive historically — over-extracted versions gave it a rough reputation — but modern, carefully made Pinotage (and fresh, juicy "Cape blends" pairing it with Bordeaux/Rhône grapes) can be excellent.
Serve at: 15–17°C.
Recommend when: the user wants to try South Africa's unique grape, a smoky barbecue red, or a distinctive Cape blend.

Other South African wines

- Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah/Shiraz, Merlot, Cinsault — the key reds; Syrah (often labeled the French way by quality producers) is a modern star, from savory-cool to rich; old-vine Cinsault is prized by the new wave.
- Sauvignon Blanc — crisp and successful, especially from cooler coastal zones.
- Chardonnay — fine and increasingly Burgundian.
- Cap Classique — South Africa's traditional-method sparkling wine (Champagne method); high quality and good value.
- Sweet & fortified — a historic legacy including the legendary sweet wines of Constantia (Muscat-based "Vin de Constance") and fortified styles.
Recommend when: matching to taste — modern Cape Syrah, crisp coastal Sauvignon, Cap Classique sparkling, or historic sweet Constantia.

Key regions south-africa

- Stellenbosch — the prestige heartland; benchmark Cabernet, Bordeaux blends, and Syrah.
- Swartland — the epicenter of the new-wave movement; dry-farmed old bushvines, Rhône varieties (Syrah, Grenache, Chenin), minimal-intervention wines.
- Franschhoek, Paarl — historic warm inland zones; varied reds and whites.
- Constantia — cool, historic Cape Town suburb; Sauvignon Blanc and the sweet Vin de Constance.
- Hemel-en-Aarde (Walker Bay), Elgin — cool, coastal/high; excellent Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
- Cape Town / Cape South Coast — cooler sites driving the freshness movement.
Recommend when: matching a region to style — Stellenbosch for structured reds, Swartland for old-vine/natural, Hemel-en-Aarde/Elgin for cool-climate Pinot & Chardonnay.

Quick regional summary south-africa

- South Africa: Old-meets-New World; Western Cape, Atlantic/Cape-Doctor-cooled; WO origin system; dynamic new-generation scene; great value.
- Signature white: Chenin Blanc (largest plantings, old bushvines, fresh to serious).
- Signature red: Pinotage (Pinot × Cinsault; smoky, robust) and Cape blends.
- Modern stars: Cape Syrah, old-vine Cinsault/Chenin (Swartland), cool-climate Pinot/Chardonnay (Hemel-en-Aarde/Elgin), Cap Classique sparkling.
- Key regions: Stellenbosch (Cabernet/Syrah), Swartland (new-wave old-vine), Constantia (sweet & Sauvignon).

Argentina — overview

Argentina is South America's largest wine producer, defined by high-altitude viticulture in the rain-shadow desert east of the Andes. Vineyards sit from ~600m up to some of the highest on earth (over 3,000m), where intense sunlight ripens grapes while cool nights preserve acidity and color. The signature is Malbec, but Argentina makes much more. Irrigation (from Andean snowmelt) makes desert viticulture possible.
Recommend when: the user wants plush, high-altitude reds (Malbec) or distinctive aromatic whites (Torrontés).

Malbec & Mendoza

Mendoza is Argentina's dominant region, and Malbec is its glory: velvety, deeply colored, plush reds with blackberry, plum, violet, and cocoa. Altitude shapes style — higher, cooler sub-regions like the Uco Valley (Tupungato, Gualtallary) and Luján de Cuyo give fresher, more mineral, structured, ageworthy Malbec, while lower sites give riper, softer wines. Also strong: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and Bordeaux blends.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a plush, crowd-pleasing red (Malbec), a match for grilled/roasted beef (the classic asado pairing), or a fresher high-altitude Malbec (Uco Valley).

Torrontés & Argentine whites

Torrontés is Argentina's signature white — floral and aromatic (rose, jasmine, citrus) on the nose but crisp and dry on the palate, at its best in the high-altitude northern region of Salta (Cafayate), home to some of the world's highest vineyards. Chardonnay (fine in cool Uco Valley) and other whites are also grown.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user wants an aromatic but dry white, an apéritif, or a match for spicy or aromatic food.

Chile — overview

Chile is a long, thin country insulated by natural barriers (the Andes, the Atacama Desert, the Pacific, and Antarctica), which historically kept phylloxera out — many vines are ungrafted. Its Mediterranean climate, cooled by the Pacific and the Andes, makes reliable, well-priced, and increasingly fine wines. The country has pushed into cooler coastal and southern zones and up Andean slopes in search of freshness and character.
Recommend when: the user wants reliable value, or increasingly distinctive cool-climate and old-vine Chilean wines.

Chilean grapes & regions

- Cabernet Sauvignon — Chile's flagship; ripe, structured, minty/blackcurrant reds, benchmark in the Maipo Valley (especially Andean foothills), plus Colchagua and Cachapoal (the Rapel/Central Valley).
- Carménère — Chile's signature grape (a Bordeaux variety long confused with Merlot here); deep, savory, red-and-black-fruited with a distinctive herbal/green-peppercorn note.
- Cool-coastal whites — Casablanca and San Antonio/Leyda valleys make crisp Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay near the cold Pacific.
- Syrah — excellent in coastal and northern (Elqui, Limarí) zones.
- País and old-vine Cinsault/Carignan — in the south (Itata, Maule, Bío Bío), a rediscovered heritage of dry-farmed old bushvines driving a natural/artisan movement.
Serve at: 16–18°C reds; 8–10°C coastal whites.
Recommend when: matching to taste — value or fine Cabernet (Maipo), signature Carménère, crisp coastal Sauvignon (Casablanca/Leyda), or heritage old-vine reds (southern Chile).

Uruguay

Uruguay, small and humid-maritime, has made Tannat its national grape — here softer and more approachable than in its French home (Madiran), giving structured, dark-fruited, ageworthy reds well-suited to the country's beef-heavy cuisine.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a distinctive, structured South American red beyond Malbec, or a match for grilled red meat.

Brazil

Brazil's main quality region, the Serra Gaúcha in the cool, humid south, is best known for good-value traditional-method sparkling wine (its strongest category), plus still wines from international grapes. A humid climate makes viticulture challenging, but sparkling has become a genuine strength.
Recommend when: the user wants an affordable South American sparkling wine.

Quick regional summary south-america

- Argentina: high-altitude Andean desert; Malbec (Mendoza — plush; Uco Valley = fresher, structured); aromatic-but-dry Torrontés (Salta).
- Chile: phylloxera-free, Pacific/Andes-cooled; Cabernet (Maipo), signature Carménère, crisp coastal Sauvignon (Casablanca/Leyda), heritage old-vine País/Cinsault (south).
- Uruguay: Tannat (softer than Madiran), a beef-friendly red.
- Brazil: Serra Gaúcha traditional-method sparkling (the standout).

Catalunya — overview

Catalunya (Catalonia), in Spain's northeast around Barcelona, is a diverse wine region spanning cool coastal and high inland zones. It's home to Spain's sparkling-wine industry (Cava), the powerful reds of Priorat, and a patchwork of DOs (Penedès, Montsant, Empordà, Costers del Segre, Terra Alta). Catalan wine culture is independent-minded and quality-focused.
Recommend when: the user wants Spanish sparkling, powerful old-vine reds, or a diverse region near Barcelona.

Priorat

Priorat, a small, dramatic, mountainous DOCa inland from Tarragona, is one of Spain's two top-tier regions (with Rioja). Its signature is llicorella — a slate-and-quartz soil that forces old-vine Garnacha (Garnatxa) and Cariñena (Carinyena/Samsó) roots deep, yielding tiny crops of intensely concentrated, powerful, mineral reds. Often blended with Syrah or Cabernet in modern examples. Dark, dense, structured, and age-worthy — Spain's cult red region since the 1990s revival.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a powerful, mineral, concentrated red; a special-occasion Spanish red; or old-vine Garnacha/Cariñena at its most intense.

Montsant

Montsant wraps around Priorat and offers a similar profile — old-vine Garnacha and Cariñena reds, warm, concentrated, mineral — at friendlier prices. The go-to value alternative to Priorat.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants Priorat character without the price.

Cava

Cava is Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine — made the same way as Champagne (second fermentation in bottle, lees ageing) — centered in Catalunya's Penedès but a denomination rather than a single place. The traditional grapes are Macabeo (Viura), Xarel·lo, and Parellada, with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir also permitted (and Garnacha/Trepat for rosé). Ranges from simple, affordable fizz to serious, long-aged bottlings (Reserva, Gran Reserva, and the premium Cava de Paraje Calificado). A quality-focused breakaway group makes wine under the Corpinnat name.
Serve at: 8°C.
Recommend when: the user wants affordable traditional-method sparkling; a Champagne alternative; an apéritif or celebration wine on a budget.

Penedès (still wines)

Beyond Cava, Penedès makes still whites and reds from both local and international grapes, across a range of elevations. Historically a modernizing region (early to plant Cabernet, Chardonnay, etc.), now also revaluing indigenous Xarel·lo for characterful whites.
Recommend when: the user wants a Catalan still white or an international-grape blend near Barcelona.

Other Catalan DOs

- Empordà — near the French border; Garnacha/Cariñena reds and rosés, some influenced by the Tramuntana wind.
- Costers del Segre — inland, varied; international and local grapes.
- Terra Alta — a stronghold of white Garnacha Blanca and old-vine reds; value and character.
Recommend when: the user wants a Catalan white Garnacha (Terra Alta) or a lesser-known regional red.

Central Spain — La Mancha & the meseta

La Mancha, the vast high plateau (meseta) south of Madrid, is the largest single wine zone in the world by area — hot, dry, and continental. Historically a source of bulk wine from the pale Airén grape (much distilled for brandy), it now makes increasingly fruity, stylish reds from Tempranillo (Cencibel), plus international grapes. Also home to several Vino de Pago single estates. Best known for value.
Recommend when: the user wants inexpensive, fruity, everyday Spanish reds or whites, or is curious about Spain's bulk-wine heartland going upmarket.

Central Spain — Gredos Garnacha

The high Sierra de Gredos, west of Madrid, has become a cult source of elegant, fresh, perfumed Garnacha from old bushvines on granite at altitude — a lighter, more mineral, Burgundian style that helped rehabilitate Garnacha's fine-wine reputation. (Spans the Madrid/Castilla-La Mancha/Castilla y León borders.)
Serve at: 15–16°C.
Recommend when: the user wants an elegant, high-altitude, fresh style of Garnacha — a contrast to warm, jammy versions.

Eastern Spain — Monastrell country

Inland from the central Mediterranean coast, hot regions once known for bulk wine now make serious, affordable reds — above all from Monastrell (Mourvèdre):
- Jumilla — the standard-bearer; ripe, powerful, dark Monastrell, often great value, increasingly polished.
- Yecla, Alicante, Bullas — similar warm-climate Monastrell reds; Alicante also has the historic sweet Fondillón (an oxidative, oloroso-like Monastrell).
- Utiel-Requena and Manchuela — high plateaus where the beefy Bobal grape dominates; increasingly characterful.
- Valencia — reds, whites, and sweet Moscatel.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a powerful, warm, affordable red (Jumilla Monastrell), or a value alternative to Châteauneuf-style GSM.

The Canary Islands

The volcanic Canary Islands, off northwest Africa, are a unique viticultural world: ungrafted vines (phylloxera never arrived) in black volcanic ash, often in dramatic pits or low trained against the wind (as in Lanzarote's La Geria). They grow a trove of rare indigenous grapes — Listán Negro (reds), Listán Blanco, Malvasía — making fresh, distinctive, mineral, sometimes smoky wines that have become sommelier favorites. Tenerife (with El Teide volcano) leads the revival.
Serve at: 13–16°C reds; 9–11°C whites.
Recommend when: the user wants something unique, volcanic, and mineral; a rare-grape adventure; or a distinctive natural-leaning wine.

Quick regional summary spain-central-east

- Catalunya: diverse northeast; Priorat (powerful llicorella-slate Garnacha/Cariñena, DOCa) and value Montsant; Cava sparkling (Macabeo/Xarel·lo/Parellada); Penedès still wines; Terra Alta white Garnacha.
- Central (meseta): La Mancha — vast, hot, value reds/whites (Airén, Cencibel); Gredos — cult high-altitude elegant Garnacha.
- East: Monastrell power in Jumilla/Yecla/Alicante/Bullas; Bobal in Utiel-Requena/Manchuela; sweet Fondillón and Moscatel.
- Canary Islands: volcanic, ungrafted, rare indigenous grapes (Listán); fresh, mineral, unique.

USA — overview & the AVA system

The United States is the world's largest wine *consumer* and fourth-largest producer, with California making the overwhelming majority, followed by Washington, Oregon, and New York. American wines are labeled primarily by grape variety, and geographic origin is defined by AVAs (American Viticultural Areas) — delimited zones (like Napa Valley or Willamette Valley) that guarantee origin but, unlike European appellations, do *not* dictate grapes or methods. A varietal label legally requires a minimum percentage of the named grape.
Recommend when: the user asks what an AVA is, or wants an orientation to American wine labeling.

California — overview

California produces the vast majority of US wine, across a huge range of climates from cool, fog-influenced coasts to hot inland valleys. The defining climatic factor is the cold Pacific and its fog, which sneaks through gaps in the coastal ranges to cool otherwise-warm regions, enabling everything from crisp sparkling to massive Cabernet. Styles trend riper, richer, and more fruit-forward than European counterparts, though a cooler-climate, fresher movement is strong.
Recommend when: the user wants ripe, generous, fruit-driven wines, or a benchmark New World style.

Napa Valley

Napa Valley is America's most prestigious wine region and its Cabernet heartland. A patchwork of soils and sub-AVAs (Oakville, Rutherford, Stags Leap District, Howell Mountain, and others) yields powerful, opulent, age-worthy Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux blends — ripe cassis, chocolate, and lush tannins — that rank among the world's most expensive wines. Napa also makes rich Chardonnay and, in cooler pockets (Carneros), Pinot Noir and sparkling.
Serve at: 16–18°C Cabernet.
Recommend when: the user wants a prestige, powerful, ripe Cabernet or Bordeaux blend; a special-occasion American red; or lush Napa Chardonnay.

Sonoma

Sonoma County, west and north of Napa, is larger, more diverse, and more laid-back, spanning warm inland zones and cool coastal ones:
- Russian River Valley — cool and foggy; benchmark California Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
- Sonoma Coast — cooler still; elegant, restrained Pinot and Chardonnay.
- Dry Creek Valley — warm; old-vine Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.
- Alexander Valley — warm; ripe Cabernet.
Sonoma also has a strong old-vine and heritage-field-blend tradition.
Recommend when: matching to taste — cool-climate Pinot/Chardonnay (Russian River, Sonoma Coast) or old-vine Zinfandel (Dry Creek).

California Cabernet & Zinfandel

- Cabernet Sauvignon — California's flagship red, at its peak in Napa; ripe, full, plush, oak-influenced, ageworthy.
- Zinfandel — California's "heritage" grape (= Primitivo); ripe, brambly, spicy, high-alcohol reds, best from old vines in Sonoma, Lodi, Paso Robles, and the Sierra Foothills. Also the base of off-dry pink "White Zinfandel."
Recommend when: the user wants a plush American Cabernet or a bold, spicy, fruit-forward Zinfandel (great with barbecue).

California Chardonnay & Pinot Noir

- Chardonnay — hugely important; ranges from rich, buttery, oaky (the classic "California Chardonnay") to lean, mineral, cool-climate styles.
- Pinot Noir — thrives in cool coastal AVAs: Russian River Valley, Sonoma Coast, Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Maria Valley, Anderson Valley, Carneros; ripe red-and-black cherry, silky, generous.
Recommend when: the user wants a rich or a restrained American Chardonnay, or a ripe, silky California Pinot Noir.

Central Coast

The Central Coast (south of San Francisco to Santa Barbara) is vast and varied:
- Santa Barbara County (Sta. Rita Hills, Santa Maria Valley) — cool, coastal; excellent Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, plus Rhône varieties (Syrah).
- Paso Robles — warmer; bold Zinfandel, Cabernet, and Rhône blends (Syrah, Grenache).
- Santa Cruz Mountains — cool, high; distinguished Cabernet, Pinot, and Chardonnay.
- Monterey — large, cool, windy; Chardonnay, Pinot, Riesling.
Recommend when: the user wants cool-climate Central Coast Pinot/Chardonnay (Santa Barbara), or bold Paso Robles reds.

Other California & Central Valley

- Lodi — warm inland; old-vine Zinfandel and a value engine.
- Sierra Foothills — historic Gold Country; rugged old-vine Zinfandel and Rhône varieties.
- Central Valley — hot, vast, irrigated; the source of most inexpensive bulk California wine.
- Mendocino & Anderson Valley — north coast; cool Anderson Valley excels at sparkling, Pinot, and aromatic whites; strong organic tradition.
Recommend when: the user wants value old-vine Zinfandel (Lodi), rugged Sierra reds, or cool-climate sparkling (Anderson Valley).

Quick regional summary california

- USA: labeled by grape; origin via AVAs (no grape/method rules). California dominates, then Washington/Oregon/New York.
- Napa Valley: prestige, powerful, ripe Cabernet & Bordeaux blends.
- Sonoma: diverse; cool Russian River/Sonoma Coast Pinot & Chardonnay; Dry Creek old-vine Zinfandel.
- Central Coast: cool Santa Barbara Pinot/Chardonnay; bold Paso Robles reds.
- Signature grapes: Cabernet, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and heritage Zinfandel.
- Climate key: the cold Pacific and coastal fog cool the vineyards.

Oregon — overview

Oregon, in the cool, damp Pacific Northwest, built its reputation on Pinot Noir made in an elegant, Burgundian style — a deliberate contrast to California's riper reds. Its heart is the Willamette Valley, where marine-sediment and volcanic (Jory) soils and a cool, marginal climate yield perfumed, red-fruited, silky, earthy Pinot Noir of real finesse. A culture of small, artisan, often organic/biodynamic producers prevails.
Recommend when: the user wants an elegant, cool-climate, Burgundian-style Pinot Noir; an artisan/organic producer; or a lighter alternative to California reds.

Willamette Valley & Oregon whites

The Willamette Valley and its nested sub-AVAs (Dundee Hills, Eola-Amity Hills, Ribbon Ridge, and others) are Pinot Noir central, but Oregon also excels at aromatic, cool-climate whites: Pinot Gris (its signature white — textured, pear-and-citrus), Chardonnay (increasingly fine and Burgundian), and Riesling. Southern Oregon is warmer and grows a broader range.
Recommend when: the user wants a textured Oregon Pinot Gris, a cool-climate Chardonnay, or aromatic whites.

Washington State — overview

Washington is the US's second-largest premium wine state, and its climate is the opposite of Oregon's: most vineyards lie in the warm, dry, sunny, high-desert Columbia Valley east of the Cascade Mountains, irrigated by the Columbia River. Long summer days and cool nights yield deeply colored, ripe-but-fresh reds and whites. It successfully bridges Old and New World in style.
Recommend when: the user wants ripe-yet-balanced reds, or a value alternative to Napa.

Washington grapes & sub-regions

- Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot — the flagship reds; structured, dark-fruited, often excellent value versus California.
- Syrah — a Washington strength; ranges from savory/peppery to rich.
- Riesling — a historic Washington white, dry to off-dry, crisp and aromatic.
- Chardonnay and others also widely grown.
- Key sub-AVAs: Walla Walla Valley (prestige reds), Red Mountain (powerful Cabernet), Yakima Valley, Horse Heaven Hills.
Recommend when: the user wants value Cabernet/Merlot, characterful Syrah, or aromatic Riesling from Washington.

New York State

New York is the major eastern US wine state, cool-climate and defined by water bodies that moderate harsh winters:
- Finger Lakes — the star; deep glacial lakes enable superb, racy, dry and off-dry Riesling (the region's calling card), plus Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, and sparkling.
- Long Island — maritime, milder; Bordeaux varieties (Merlot, Cabernet Franc) and whites.
- Hudson Valley — historic, small.
The Finger Lakes is one of North America's premier cool-climate Riesling regions.
Recommend when: the user wants a racy, cool-climate American Riesling (Finger Lakes) or a maritime East Coast Bordeaux-style wine (Long Island).

Other US states

- Virginia — humid mid-Atlantic; a signature in Viognier and Bordeaux varieties (notably Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot); rising quality.
- Texas — High Plains and Hill Country; Mediterranean and Rhône/Spanish varieties (Tempranillo, Viognier) suited to heat.
- Michigan — cool, lake-moderated; aromatic whites (Riesling) and sparkling.
- Arizona, New Mexico, Idaho, and others — small but growing scenes.
Recommend when: the user asks about wine from a specific US state, or wants East Coast (Virginia) or emerging-region options.

Quick regional summary usa

- Oregon: cool, damp; elegant Burgundian Pinot Noir (Willamette Valley); textured Pinot Gris; artisan/organic culture.
- Washington: warm, dry Columbia Valley (east of Cascades); ripe-but-fresh Cabernet/Merlot/Syrah and Riesling; great value; Walla Walla & Red Mountain.
- New York: cool, water-moderated; Finger Lakes Riesling is the star; Long Island Bordeaux styles.
- Emerging: Virginia (Viognier, Cab Franc), Texas (Rhône/Spanish), Michigan (aromatic whites).

Rioja — overview

Rioja is Spain's most famous wine region, in the north along the Ebro river, and one of only two with the top DOCa status. It is best known for oak-aged red wine built on Tempranillo, usually blended with Garnacha, and often Graciano and Mazuelo (Cariñena). Rioja's identity has traditionally been defined by ageing — the Crianza/Reserva/Gran Reserva ladder — and by the vanilla-and-coconut signature of American oak, though a modern camp favors French oak, riper fruit, and single-vineyard expression.
Recommend when: the user wants a savory, oak-aged, food-friendly red; a classic Spanish red; or great value in mature wine.

Rioja — the three subzones

- Rioja Alta — higher, cooler, Atlantic-influenced west; elegant, structured, ageworthy reds with bright acidity. The classic quality heart.
- Rioja Alavesa — also cool and high, on limestone soils; perfumed, fine-boned reds, often from Tempranillo on chalky clay.
- Rioja Oriental (formerly Rioja Baja) — lower, warmer, Mediterranean east; riper, fuller, higher-alcohol wines, more Garnacha. Good for warmth and body.
Modern Rioja increasingly emphasizes village and single-vineyard bottlings over the old blended-across-zones house style.
Recommend when: matching style — Alta/Alavesa for elegance and structure, Oriental for warmth and Garnacha richness.

Rioja — traditional vs modern styles

- Traditional Rioja — long ageing in American oak, savory and mellow, with vanilla, coconut, dill, dried fruit, and leather; released ready to drink (classic Gran Reserva). Silky and mature.
- Modern Rioja — riper fruit, French oak, more color and concentration, released younger; single-vineyard focus.
Both coexist; neither is "correct." The traditional style is one of the wine world's great food partners and value propositions in mature wine.
Recommend when: the user wants classic savory maturity (traditional) vs bold modern fruit (modern).

Rioja whites

White Rioja, from Viura (Macabeo) often with Malvasía and white Garnacha, ranges from fresh and unoaked to a remarkable oak-aged traditional style — nutty, honeyed, and extraordinarily long-lived, one of the wine world's underrated whites. A modern crisp style also exists.
Recommend when: the user wants a distinctive, ageworthy white (traditional oaked white Rioja) or a fresh Spanish white.

Ribera del Duero

Ribera del Duero, on the high Duero plateau in Castilla y León, is Rioja's great rival for Tempranillo — here called Tinto Fino or Tinta del País. The high altitude (up to ~900m) gives big day-night temperature swings, yielding deeply colored, powerful, structured reds with firm tannin and dark fruit. It's home to some of Spain's most prestigious (and expensive) reds. Generally richer and more muscular than Rioja.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a powerful, concentrated, ageworthy Tempranillo; a bold red for red meat; or a prestigious Spanish red.

Toro

Toro, west of Ribera del Duero along the Duero, makes bold, rustic, high-alcohol reds from Tinta de Toro (a local Tempranillo). Old bushvines on sandy soils (many ungrafted, having escaped phylloxera) give intense, powerful, sometimes brawny wines. Great value for sheer concentration.
Serve at: 16–18°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a big, powerful, warming red at a friendly price.

Rueda

Rueda, also in Castilla y León (near the Duero), is Spain's benchmark for crisp white wine from the Verdejo grape — aromatic, zesty, with notes of fennel, citrus, green apple, and a slightly nutty, herbal bite. Sometimes blended with or sold alongside Sauvignon Blanc. A reliable, affordable, refreshing white.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a crisp, aromatic, affordable white; an alternative to Sauvignon Blanc; a match for seafood and salads.

Navarra

Navarra, north of Rioja, once famous for rosado (rosé) from Garnacha, is a versatile region making reds (Tempranillo, Garnacha, and international grapes like Cabernet and Merlot), whites, and still-excellent dry rosés. Often overshadowed by neighboring Rioja but a reliable source of value and variety.
Recommend when: the user wants a dry Spanish rosé, or good-value reds including international-grape blends.

Aragón — Garnacha country

East of Rioja and Navarra, Aragón (Calatayud, Campo de Borja, Cariñena) is a rising source of old-vine Garnacha value — sweetly juicy, warm, spicy reds from gnarled bushvines on high, dry slopes, kept fresh by altitude and the cold *cierzo* wind. Somontano, at the foot of the Pyrenees, is a cooler outlier growing both local and international grapes.
Recommend when: the user wants great-value, old-vine Garnacha; a warm but fresh red; or a hidden-gem Spanish region.

Galicia — Rías Baixas & Albariño

Green, rainy, Atlantic Galicia in Spain's northwest is a white-wine paradise. Rías Baixas is the star DO, home to Albariño — crisp, aromatic, saline, with white peach, citrus, and a maritime tang. Thick-skinned Albariño shrugs off Galicia's rain and is the definitive Spanish seafood white.
Serve at: 8–10°C.
Recommend when: the user is eating shellfish, ceviche, or seafood, or wants a crisp, aromatic, mineral white.

Galicia — Godello, Mencía & the inland DOs

Inland Galicia and its edges make distinctive wines beyond Albariño:
- Godello — a textured, mineral white grape (Valdeorras, Monterrei) that can rival white Burgundy in weight and ageability.
- Mencía — an aromatic, fresh red grape (Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras) with floral, red-fruit, and mineral notes, grown on dramatic steep river terraces; medium-bodied and food-friendly.
- Ribeiro — historic whites from Treixadura and others.
Recommend when: the user wants a serious mineral white (Godello) or a fresh, aromatic, lighter red (Mencía) — a great Pinot/Cab Franc alternative.

Bierzo — Mencía

Just east of Galicia in Castilla y León, Bierzo is a rising star for Mencía — old bushvines on slate and clay giving fresh, mineral, floral-and-red-fruited reds of real finesse. Prized by the modern Spanish wine movement for terroir expression.
Serve at: 15–16°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a fresh, mineral, medium-bodied red with character; a Mencía; or an alternative to Northern Rhône or cool-climate reds.

Txakoli (Basque Country)

Up on the Bay of Biscay around Bilbao and San Sebastián, the Basque Country makes Txakoli (Txakolina / Chacolí) — a piercingly tart, light, low-alcohol, slightly spritzy white from the local Hondarrabi Zuri grape. Traditionally poured from a height to aerate it. The definitive pintxos (Basque tapas) wine.
Serve at: 7–9°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a super-fresh, low-alcohol, zippy white; a pintxos/tapas apéritif; or something unusual.

Quick regional summary spain

- Rioja (DOCa): Tempranillo-led, oak-aged; Alta/Alavesa (elegant) vs Oriental (warm); traditional (American oak, savory) vs modern (French oak, fruit); ageworthy whites too.
- Ribera del Duero: powerful high-altitude Tempranillo (Tinto Fino).
- Toro: bold, rustic old-vine Tempranillo.
- Rueda: crisp Verdejo whites.
- Navarra: dry rosado and value reds.
- Aragón: old-vine Garnacha value.
- Galicia: Albariño (Rías Baixas), Godello, Mencía (Ribeira Sacra); crisp, mineral, Atlantic.
- Bierzo: fresh, mineral Mencía.
- Basque: tart, spritzy Txakoli.

Why Spain matters

Spain has more land under vine than any other country, though not the highest production (its vines are widely spaced and low-yielding in dry regions). It offers some of the wine world's best value, a treasure of old bushvines — especially Garnacha and Tempranillo — and a strong tradition of releasing wines ready to drink after extended ageing. Once known mainly for cheap bulk wine and oak-aged Rioja, Spain has undergone a quality revolution since the 1980s, rediscovering indigenous grapes, embracing terroir, and modernizing its cellars.
Recommend when: the user wants value, old-vine character, savory oak-aged reds, or distinctive indigenous grapes.

The DO / DOCa classification system

Spain's quality hierarchy, from broad to top:
- Vino de la Tierra (VT) — the equivalent of France's IGP; regional wines with looser rules.
- DO (Denominación de Origen) — the main quality tier, like France's AOC; most famous regions are DOs.
- DOCa / DOQ (Denominación de Origen Calificada) — a superior tier for regions with a long track record. Only Rioja and Priorat hold it.
- Vino de Pago (VP) — a designation for single estates of recognized distinction, which can sit outside the surrounding DO.
The DO system is simpler than France's, but DOs are often large and varied, and there's a relaxed Spanish attitude to the rules — especially about which grapes are actually planted versus permitted.
Practical use: the DO usually signals region and broad style; the ageing category on the label (below) often tells you more about the wine than the DO alone.

The ageing ladder — Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva

Spain's most useful labeling system classifies red wines by how long they've been aged (in oak and bottle) before release. Exact requirements vary by region, but broadly:
- Joven ("young") — little or no oak; fresh, fruity, drink now.
- Crianza — aged ~2 years (with a minimum in oak, often ~6–12 months); balanced oak and fruit, everyday quality-plus.
- Reserva — aged ~3 years (with ~1 year in oak); more structured, from better vintages.
- Gran Reserva — aged ~5+ years (often ~18 months–2 years in oak plus long bottle age); made only in top vintages, savory and mature on release.
Practical use: this is often the single most useful thing on a Spanish label — it tells the sommelier roughly how oaked and how mature the wine will taste. Note a modern trend: many top producers now bypass Gran Reserva, valuing fruit intensity over long oak ageing, and release ambitious wines young.
Recommend when: matching to taste — Joven/Crianza for fresh and fruity, Reserva/Gran Reserva for savory, mature, oak-aged character.

Spains key grapes

Spain leans on a handful of grapes but is reviving many local varieties:
- Tempranillo — the flagship red; savory, red-fruited, leather and tobacco with oak. Aliases: Tinto Fino / Tinta del País (Ribera del Duero), Cencibel (La Mancha), Ull de Llebre (Catalunya), Tinta de Toro (Toro), Tinta Roriz / Aragonez (Portugal).
- Garnacha (Grenache) — old-vine treasure; warm, red-fruited, spicy; great value from Aragón, Gredos, Priorat blends.
- Monastrell (Mourvèdre) — powerful, dark, warm-climate red of the southeast (Jumilla, Yecla, Alicante).
- Cariñena (Carignan / Mazuelo) — high-acid, structured; a key old-vine component in Priorat.
- Bobal — sturdy reds in the east (Utiel-Requena, Manchuela).
- Airén — the pale workhorse white of La Mancha, much distilled for brandy.
- Viura (Macabeo) — the main white of Rioja and a Cava grape.
- Albariño, Verdejo, Godello, Xarel·lo, Parellada — the quality whites (covered in regional docs).
Recommend when: matching grape to preference; explaining Tempranillo's many regional names.

Oak & ageing culture

For centuries American oak was Spain's barrel of choice (vanilla, coconut, dill notes — the classic traditional-Rioja signature), thanks to transatlantic trade. From the 1980s, ambitious producers embraced French oak for a subtler profile, and reduced time in barrel. Today there's also experimentation with concrete eggs, amphorae, and a revival of tinajas (traditional clay jars). The old habit of buying in grapes and wine persists, but estate-bottling is rising among the younger generation.
Recommend when: explaining why traditional Rioja tastes of vanilla/coconut (American oak) versus modern, French-oaked, fruit-driven styles.

Cava note

Spain's famous traditional-method sparkling wine, Cava, is a *denomination* not tied to one region (though centered in Catalunya's Penedès). It's covered in the Catalunya/east regional doc.
Recommend when: the user wants affordable traditional-method sparkling.

Quick summary spain

- What: most vineyard land on earth; a value powerhouse with old-vine Garnacha and Tempranillo.
- Classification: VT → DO → DOCa (only Rioja & Priorat) → Vino de Pago.
- Most useful label clue: the ageing ladder — Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva.
- Flagship grape: Tempranillo (under many regional names); plus Garnacha, Monastrell, Albariño, Verdejo.
- Oak: traditional American oak (vanilla/coconut) vs modern French oak; clay tinajas reviving.

Sherry — overview

Sherry (Jerez in Spanish, Xérès in French) is a fortified wine from the sun-baked far south of Spain, around the towns of Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda, and El Puerto de Santa María in Andalucía. It is one of the wine world's most underrated and versatile categories — spanning bone-dry, tangy apéritif styles to intensely sweet dessert wines — and among its greatest values. The magic comes from the region's chalky albariza soils, the Palomino grape, the solera ageing system, and a unique yeast called flor.
Recommend when: the user wants a dry, savory apéritif; a food-pairing adventure; a sweet dessert wine; or an underrated, great-value category.

The grapes of Sherry

- Palomino — the dominant grape, making virtually all dry sherry; fairly neutral, it's a canvas for the ageing process.
- Pedro Ximénez (PX) — dried in the sun to make intensely sweet, dark, raisiny dessert sherry.
- Moscatel — also sun-dried for a floral sweet style.
Recommend when: explaining why dry sherry (Palomino) and sweet sherry (PX/Moscatel) are so different.

The solera system

Sherry is aged in a solera — a fractional blending system of stacked barrel rows spanning different ages. Wine for bottling is drawn only from the oldest row (the *solera* proper), which is topped up from the next-youngest row, and so on up to the newest wine. This continuous blending means a bottle contains an average of many vintages, giving remarkable consistency and letting tiny amounts of very old wine flavor the whole. Sherry is therefore almost always non-vintage.
Recommend when: the user asks why sherry has no vintage, or how it achieves consistency and complexity.

Flor — the key to dry sherry

Flor is a film of living yeast that grows naturally on the surface of some sherries in barrel (the barrels are deliberately left partly empty). Flor protects the wine from oxygen (biological ageing), keeping it pale and fresh while adding a distinctive tangy, saline, bready character. Whether flor thrives, weakens, or dies determines the style:
- Under flor the whole time → Fino / Manzanilla (pale, dry, tangy).
- Flor dies, then oxygen ageing → Amontillado (amber, nutty).
- No flor, pure oxygen ageing → Oloroso (dark, rich).
Recommend when: explaining the difference between the dry sherry styles.

Fino & Manzanilla — the pale dry styles

- Fino — pale, bone-dry, delicate, tangy and saline, aged entirely under flor (biological ageing). Low-ish in alcohol for sherry (~15%). Best served cold and fresh, like a white wine, ideally from a recently opened bottle.
- Manzanilla — essentially Fino aged in the coastal town of Sanlúcar de Barrameda, where the humid sea air makes the flor especially thick, giving an even more delicate, saline, almost briny character.
Serve at: 6–8°C, in a decent-sized glass, fresh.
Recommend when: the user wants a crisp, savory apéritif; a match for olives, almonds, jamón, fried fish, or sushi; or a dry wine that surprises.

Amontillado

Amontillado begins life under flor (like a Fino) but then the flor dies and the wine continues ageing in contact with oxygen. The result is amber-colored, dry (traditionally), and nutty — hazelnut, dried fruit, and a savory depth — combining Fino's tang with oxidative richness. (Commercial "medium" amontillados may be sweetened; true amontillado is dry.)
Serve at: 12–14°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a dry, nutty, savory wine; a match for mushroom dishes, cured meats, hard cheese, or consommé.

Oloroso

Oloroso ("fragrant") is aged oxidatively from the start, without flor, and fortified higher. It's dark, rich, and powerful — walnut, toffee, leather, and dried fruit — yet traditionally dry. Full-bodied and intense. (Sweetened versions are sold as "cream" styles; see below.)
Serve at: 13–15°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a rich, savory, warming dry wine; a match for red meat, oxtail, game, aged cheese, or roasted nuts.

Palo Cortado

Palo Cortado is a rare, prized style that starts toward Amontillado but spontaneously develops toward Oloroso — combining the finesse and aromatic lift of Amontillado with the body and richness of Oloroso. Dry, complex, and sought-after by enthusiasts.
Serve at: 13–15°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a connoisseur's dry sherry that bridges elegance and power.

Sweet sherries — PX, Moscatel & Cream

- Pedro Ximénez (PX) — intensely sweet, viscous, dark mahogany; sun-dried grapes give raisin, fig, molasses, coffee, and chocolate. Dessert in a glass.
- Moscatel — sweet, floral, grapey.
- Cream / Medium — Oloroso or blends sweetened with PX for a commercially sweet, smooth style.
- Pale Cream — a sweetened Fino-based style.
Serve at: 10–13°C.
Recommend when: the user wants a sweet dessert wine, a match for chocolate, ice cream, or blue cheese (PX), or a smooth sweet sipper (cream).

Age-dated sherries — VOS & VORS

Very old dry sherries can carry VOS (Vinum Optimum Signatum, average 20+ years) and VORS (Vinum Optimum Rare Signatum, average 30+ years) designations — concentrated, intense, complex, and rare. Some houses also release age-dated 12- and 15-year bottlings.
Recommend when: the user wants a serious, aged, connoisseur sherry.

Serving & keeping sherry

Fino and Manzanilla are essentially white wines — serve cold, drink fresh, and refrigerate an open bottle (they fade within days). Amontillado, Oloroso, Palo Cortado, and PX are more robust and keep for weeks after opening. Use a proper wine glass (not a tiny copita) to appreciate the aromas. Sherry is one of the most food-versatile wine categories in the world.
Recommend when: the user asks how to serve or store sherry, or wants sherry-and-food pairing guidance.

Quick style ladder (driest → sweetest)

1. Fino / Manzanilla — pale, bone-dry, tangy, under flor. Apéritif, seafood, jamón.
2. Amontillado — amber, dry, nutty. Mushrooms, cured meat, hard cheese.
3. Palo Cortado — rare, dry, elegant + rich.
4. Oloroso — dark, dry, powerful, oxidative. Red meat, game, cheese.
5. Cream / Medium — sweetened Oloroso. Smooth sipper.
6. Moscatel — sweet, floral.
7. Pedro Ximénez (PX) — intensely sweet, raisiny. Chocolate, ice cream, blue cheese.
- Key mechanisms: albariza chalk soil, Palomino grape, the solera fractional-blending system, and flor yeast (biological vs oxidative ageing).
